title: Judge every ad and email by cost per purchase, not clicks or likes
hypothesis: If we pick winning ads by cost per purchase instead of CTR or opens, then spend stops rewarding copy that only earns attention because the team is no longer misled by a high click rate that hides a low buy rate.

signal.check: Ads or emails are ranked and picked as winners by CTR, opens or likes, and cost per purchase is not the first column reviewers look at.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source notes mystery-style copy raised CTR about 18% while lowering purchases in one uncited study

risk.note: Changes how winners are judged, not the copy itself.

prerequisites: Cost per purchase or conversion data by ad or send
steps: Pull the current ranking of ads or emails by CTR, opens or likes.
Re-rank the same list by cost per purchase or purchase conversion rate.
Pick the next round of winners from the purchase-ranked list.
Flag any ad with a high click rate but a low purchase rate for a copy rewrite.

test.method: Compare the CTR ranking and the cost-per-purchase ranking for the same ad set or send.
test.read_point: After the set has enough spend to report cost per purchase reliably.

title: Run the salesman test on every line before it ships
hypothesis: If every line in an ad must pass as something you would say to one interested buyer face to face, then weak lines drop out because slogans, jokes and decoration fail the test and get cut.

signal.check: The draft has lines that read as slogans, wordplay or filler rather than something a person would say to a real buyer.

risk.note: A wording filter; no product or price change.

steps: Read each line as if saying it to one named buyer standing in front of you.
Cut any line that would sound like a slogan, joke or boast in person.
Rewrite the cut lines as something you would actually say to close the sale.

test.method: Have a second person read the draft aloud as if pitching one buyer and mark any line that feels off.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships, then compare cost per purchase after send.

title: Write to one named shopper on the exact device named in the brief
hypothesis: If the writer pictures one named shopper on the device the brief names before drafting, then the copy fits the moment better because it is written for a real person and screen, not an average visitor.

signal.check: The brief has no named shopper, segment or device, and the draft reads like it was written for everyone.

risk.note: A briefing step, not a copy risk.

prerequisites: Segment or avatar notes for the product
steps: Name the shopper: who they are, what is in their cart already, and the device (phone feed, PDP, inbox).
Write the top 20 to 35 percent segment that visits and pays most, not a generic average visitor.
Draft with that one person in mind and re-read for anything that only fits 'everyone'.

test.method: Write two versions, one for a named shopper and one generic, and compare on the same audience.
test.read_point: After the test ad set or send reaches enough volume to compare.

title: Open every sentence with the reader, never I, we, our or the brand name
hypothesis: If sentences lead with the reader instead of the brand, then attention holds longer because Starch's readership research found more than half of readers ignore ads that open by bragging about the company.

signal.check: Sentences in the draft start with I, we, our, the brand name or the product name instead of the reader.

expected_effect.size: more than half of readers ignore company-bragging ads in a cited readership study

risk.note: A rewrite rule; nothing to roll back beyond wording.

steps: Scan the draft for every sentence that starts with I, we, our, the brand name or the product name.
Flip each one to start with you or the reader's situation.
Keep the one allowed exception: a launch line like 'Introducing: [product]' when the brand wants to name it on purpose.

test.method: Count reader-first vs brand-first sentence starts before and after the edit.
test.read_point: After the edited version runs against the brand-first version.

title: Write short sentences for a thumb scrolling a phone and hit a 7th-grade reading score
hypothesis: If sentences stay short and simple enough to score a Flesch Reading Ease of 70 or higher, then more readers finish the copy because scanning a phone screen punishes long, hard sentences.

signal.check: A readability score run on the draft comes back below Flesch 70, or sentences average well over 11 words.

risk.note: A wording pass computed in code, not the model.

prerequisites: A readability scoring tool or script
steps: Run the draft through a Flesch Reading Ease score in code.
Shorten sentences and swap long words for short ones until the score is 70 or higher.
Vary sentence length so the result does not read like a robot.
Keep the result below the ecomOS floor of tenth grade at all times.

test.method: Score the draft before and after the edit with the same tool.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Cut cleverness, jokes and boasting from sales copy by default
hypothesis: If copy drops jokes, wordplay and boasts by default, then it reads as a real sales pitch instead of entertainment because readers do not patronise a clown and boasting is a phrase pattern sources link to failed ads.
does_not_apply_when: A brand whose whole persona is built on humor, tested and working

signal.check: The draft has a joke, pun, or a line boasting about the company ('we're the best', 'insist on') instead of a buyer benefit.

expected_effect.size: roughly 80 percent of one source's plain benefit emails outperform gimmick emails in his own practice

risk.note: A tone rule; watch for a brand where wit is the tested voice.

steps: Scan the draft for jokes, wordplay, and self-congratulating lines.
Cut or rewrite each one into a plain, specific buyer benefit.
Keep wit only where a true contrast in the product creates it, not as decoration.

test.method: Run a plain, benefit-led version against a witty version on the same audience.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend or sends to compare.

title: Keep one idea per sentence and one idea per asset
hypothesis: If each sentence and each asset carries exactly one idea, then the reader understands and can be persuaded because a scope word like 'and' signals a weaker, split argument.

signal.check: A sentence or an ad tries to make two points joined by 'and', or the asset argues more than one idea at once.

risk.note: A drafting rule.

steps: Read each sentence and flag any joined by 'and' that could split into two ideas.
Read the whole asset and state its argument in one sentence.
If a second idea is strong, move it to its own variant or asset instead of adding it here.

test.method: Ask someone who has not seen the brief to state the asset's argument in one sentence.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Match proof depth to purchase price: one cue for impulse, full case for considered buys
hypothesis: If low-AOV impulse SKUs lead on one image and one cue while high-AOV, subscription or considered SKUs add specs, reviews and comparison before the ask, then conversion rises because central-route buyers on costly items need facts and peripheral-route buyers on cheap items need only a pleasant cue.

signal.check: A high-AOV or considered product's ad or page has only one image and a slogan with no reviews, specs or comparison, or a low-AOV impulse product's ad is buried in specs.

expected_effect.size: unknown; general split not itself sourced, but the Elaboration Likelihood Model behind it is

risk.note: A structure choice per SKU, not a claim risk.

prerequisites: AOV and product type known for the SKU
steps: Tag the SKU as low-AOV impulse or high-AOV considered.
For low-AOV impulse: lead with one strong image and one clear cue; keep basic data but do not pile on proof.
For high-AOV, subscription or considered: add a spec table, reviews, and a comparison before the CTA.
Check that the proof density matches the price, not a house default template.

test.method: Run a light-proof and a full-proof version of the same ad for the SKU and compare.
test.read_point: After each version reaches enough spend to compare cost per purchase.

title: Base every message on customer research, not the maker's own taste
hypothesis: If copy is drawn from what customers actually say rather than the founder's own logic, then it lands better because the maker is too close to the product to judge what buyers want.

signal.check: The brief or draft leans on the founder's opinion of the product with no customer language, reviews or tickets behind it.

risk.note: A research discipline, not a copy risk.

prerequisites: Reviews, tickets or chat logs available
steps: Before drafting, pull customer reviews, tickets or chat questions for the product.
Write down the customer's own words for the problem, the result and the doubt.
Never ask the founder or the team to approve copy on taste alone; use their input only to inform it.

test.method: Compare a draft built from customer language against one built from the founder's own pitch.
test.read_point: After each version runs to a comparable audience.

title: Compile the brand's own material into one reference document before writing
hypothesis: If the brand's sayings, angles, offer, critique of alternatives and proof stories are compiled into one document first, then later copy jobs move faster and stay on-voice because the writer draws from real brand material instead of inventing it each time.

signal.check: No single document exists with the brand's common phrases, angles, offer, critique of alternatives and proof stories; each job starts from a blank page.

risk.note: A one-time document build.

prerequisites: Access to brand posts, emails, packaging and support replies
steps: Collect the brand's common sayings, angles, and how their posts or videos open.
Record the current offer, including any backend offers.
Write the brand's own critique of the alternatives buyers consider.
Add stories that show a belief shift and lines that prove the brand understands the buyer.
Note how people typically join the list or first buy.
Steal the ideas from this document, never the exact words, into future copy.

test.method: Time how long the next copy job takes with the document versus the last job without one.
test.read_point: After the next two copy jobs for the brand.

title: Mine 5-star and 1-star reviews for the exact phrases customers use
hypothesis: If copy uses the exact words from 5-star and 1-star reviews for the problem, the result and the doubt, then it feels more believable to shoppers because it mirrors the language they already use to describe the same experience.

signal.check: The brand has reviews but no list of at least 20 exact customer phrases pulled from them for problem, result and doubt.

risk.note: A research step; if no reviews exist yet, use analogous product reviews and mark them as such.

prerequisites: At least some reviews, or analogous product reviews if none exist
steps: Read the brand's 5-star reviews and record exact phrases for the result and the delight.
Read the 1-star reviews and record exact phrases for the problem and the doubt.
Add support tickets and chat questions to the same list.
Stop once the list holds at least 20 phrases.
Use these phrases directly in headlines, hooks and objection lines.

test.method: Write one version using mined customer phrases and one using the writer's own words, run both.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Run 12 to 15 buyer interviews before writing a new product's copy
hypothesis: If the team runs 12 to 15 one-on-one buyer interviews before writing a new product's copy, then the copy covers the real pains because that many interviews surface about 80 percent of a segment's pains.
does_not_apply_when: A variant on copy for a product the brand already has strong review and ticket data for

signal.check: A brand-new product or segment has no interviews, only assumptions about why people will buy.

expected_effect.size: 12 to 15 interviews surface about 80 percent of a segment's pains, citing one source book

risk.note: Time cost only; no product change.

prerequisites: Access to at least 12 to 15 real or prospective buyers
steps: Recruit at least 12 buyers or prospective buyers for a short conversation.
Ask open questions about the problem, what they tried before, and their doubts.
Do not use the interviews to confirm what the team already believes; note the surprises.
Compile the findings before analysing them; wait until at least 12 are done.

test.method: Compare a copy draft written with interview findings against one without, on the same audience.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Build one feature-and-benefit table per product line
hypothesis: If every feature, including small ones, gets a real buyer benefit in a shared table, then copy stops listing features with no payoff because each row is forced through a 'you benefit by' test before it can be used.

signal.check: No feature-and-benefit table exists for the product line, or the existing one lists features with no benefit column filled in.

risk.note: A planning document.

prerequisites: Product facts with numbers from the brand record
steps: List every feature of the product line, including small ones.
For each, write 'You benefit by...' then ask 'what's the benefit of that?' until reaching the end value.
Add rows for how the brand does what it does (sourcing, values, process).
Cut any feature that gets no real benefit.
Rank the rows high, medium or low by how much they matter to the buyer.
Flag rows that only apply to some sizes or colors.

test.method: Check that every kept row has a benefit tied to a fact or number before copy is drafted from it.
test.read_point: Before the table is used for the next copy job.

title: Hunt the keystone fact and the untold process facts behind the product
hypothesis: If the writer finds the one fact nobody has told and the ordinary process steps behind the product, then the copy earns more trust because specific, unheard-of facts read as proof while 'everyone does this' reads as nothing.

signal.check: The draft leans on generic quality words with no specific process fact, number or sourcing detail behind them.

risk.note: A research step.

prerequisites: Access to production, sourcing or QC steps with real numbers
steps: Walk the making or sourcing process with someone who does it, not the marketing team.
Record each step with its real number: how often, how many, how deep, how long.
Ignore any step the team dismisses as 'everyone does this'.
Ask 'what is obvious to me that my market knows little about?' and write the answer down.
Find at least 3 process facts with numbers before drafting.

test.method: Run a version with a keystone process fact against a version with a generic quality claim.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Audit competitor messaging for baseline and white noise, never copy their text
hypothesis: If the team audits up to 10 competitor pages and ads for their top messages and CTAs, then the brand can tell what is expected baseline versus a real opening because tallying frequent messages shows what every rival already says.

signal.check: No competitor audit exists before positioning a new product or angle, so the team cannot tell a distinctive claim from category-wide white noise.

risk.note: Never save or reuse competitor sentences as copy; layout and mood only.

prerequisites: Access to the Meta Ad Library and competitor sites
steps: Find the top 3 organic and paid results per key phrase in the category.
Audit up to 10 pages, recording 5 items each: value proposition, top messages, primary CTA, reasons to buy, standouts.
Tally which messages repeat across competitors.
Check the Ads Library for long-running ads as a format signal.
Record layout and mood notes only; delete any saved competitor sentence.

test.method: Check the new copy against the tally: does it repeat category white noise or say something distinct?
test.read_point: Before the new positioning ships.

title: Find the real rival: a habit or an old way, not just another brand
hypothesis: If copy positions against the buyer's real alternative, whether a habit, a home-made fix or doing nothing, then it reaches more of the category because most non-buyers are not comparing brands, they are comparing the product to their current habit.

signal.check: Copy assumes the buyer is comparing 'us vs other brands' when most of the category is not buying any brand yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source's pork-and-beans case found only 4 percent of a category had switched from a home habit to any brand

risk.note: A framing choice.

prerequisites: Review or survey data on what buyers did before
steps: Check review and survey data for what the buyer used or did before this product.
Write down whether the real rival is a habit, a home-made fix, another brand, or doing nothing.
Frame the contrast against that real rival, not an assumed brand competitor.

test.method: Run a version framed against the real rival (habit or old way) against a version framed against 'other brands'.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Write the segment and awareness stage before choosing the lead
hypothesis: If the writer names the segment that visits and pays most, and which of the 5 awareness stages the traffic is in, before choosing a lead, then the copy opens at the right depth because a cold visitor and a returning buyer need different starting points.

signal.check: The brief does not say which segment or awareness stage the traffic is in before drafting begins.

risk.note: A briefing step.

prerequisites: Traffic source and list-join data, or a reasonable estimate
steps: Identify which segment visits most and pays most.
Pick the awareness stage the traffic is in: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, or most aware.
Note how list members joined (buyer, discount sign-up, referral).
Choose the lead's depth to match: short argument for cold traffic, fuller case for warmer traffic.

test.method: Write leads matched to two different awareness stages and run each to its matching audience.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Read research for surprises, not to confirm what the team already believes
hypothesis: If research notes are re-read specifically for surprising or repeated findings instead of confirmation, then the copy avoids the appeal the team likes best but that rarely proves the strongest.

signal.check: Research notes are used to justify a lead the team already wanted to write, with no surprising finding highlighted.

risk.note: A review-process step.

prerequisites: Completed research notes or interview transcripts
steps: Re-read the research notes a second time looking only for surprises and repeats.
List anything that contradicts what the team assumed going in.
Check whether the team's favourite appeal is actually the one supported most, or just the one they like.

test.method: Compare the appeal the team preferred before research against the appeal the surprise-and-repeat pass surfaced.
test.read_point: Before the appeal is picked for the next asset.

title: Pick one idea per SKU or collection, never one idea for the whole store
hypothesis: If each SKU or collection gets its own single selling idea instead of the store sharing one idea everywhere, then each ad argues more clearly because most top offers in one review were built on a single concept, not several.
does_not_apply_when: A true hero-SKU brand may hold one idea across the account

signal.check: Multiple SKUs or collections share the exact same headline idea, or one ad tries to carry a second idea for a different product.

expected_effect.size: 91 of a reviewer's top 100 offers centred on 1 concept in a second-hand account

risk.note: A planning discipline, not a claim risk.

prerequisites: A feature-and-benefit table and candidate ideas per SKU
steps: For a catalogue brand, list a hero product per cycle and give it its own idea.
Cut any candidate idea from the SKU's ad that cannot serve that one idea.
Check that the idea used for one SKU is not silently reused for an unrelated SKU.

test.method: Have someone unfamiliar with the brief state each SKU's ad idea in one sentence; check they differ where the SKUs differ.
test.read_point: Before the ad set for each SKU ships.

title: Test each candidate idea for easy-to-understand, easy-to-believe and unique before picking one
hypothesis: If every candidate selling idea is filtered through 3 questions (is it easy to understand, is it easy to believe, is it interesting or unique) before drafting, then the final idea holds up better because weak ideas are cut before time is spent writing them.

signal.check: The team commits to a selling idea without checking whether it is easy to understand, easy to believe, and distinct.

risk.note: A selection filter before drafting.

prerequisites: A list of candidate ideas from the feature-and-benefit table
steps: List every candidate idea and selling point from the feature-and-benefit table.
For each, ask: is it easy to understand? Easy to believe? Interesting or unique?
Drop any idea that fails one of the 3 tests.
Pick the strongest survivor as the one idea for the asset.

test.method: Have a person outside the project run the 3-question filter independently and compare picks.
test.read_point: Before the idea is handed to the writer.

title: Write the buying question: the belief the reader holds now and the belief they need to buy
hypothesis: If the writer states the reader's current belief and the belief they must reach before drafting, then the copy argues toward a clear finish line because you cannot start a persuasion race in the middle.

signal.check: The brief has no stated current belief or target belief; the writer starts drafting straight from the product's features.

risk.note: A briefing step.

prerequisites: Segment and awareness stage from R16
steps: Write the reader's current belief in their own words.
Write the belief they must hold to buy.
For a warm store list, use the store version: do these work, how, and why these rather than others.
Never write a line that tells the reader they are wrong; change the belief's focus or importance instead.

test.method: Check the finished draft moves the reader from the stated current belief to the stated target belief.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Pick one dominant appeal the product can credibly satisfy and hold every variant to it
hypothesis: If the team picks one appeal the product truly satisfies and tests other appeals separately instead of mixing several, then each variant argues more clearly because a message that targets a real pain outperforms a scattershot pitch.

signal.check: The draft mixes several different desires or pains in one asset instead of committing to one the product truly satisfies.

risk.note: An appeal-selection step.

prerequisites: Reviews or past ad results showing which desire buyers name
steps: List the desires or pains reviews and past ads show buyers naming for this product.
Pick the one the product can honestly and fully satisfy.
State the appeal in one sentence before writing.
Hold every line and every variant in the asset to that one appeal; test a different appeal in a separate variant.

test.method: Run 2 ad variants, each built on a different single appeal, and compare.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend to compare.

title: Lead the headline claim with what appeals to the most buyers in the segment
hypothesis: If the headline leads with the claim that appeals to the widest slice of the chosen segment and keeps narrow claims in the body, then more of the targeted traffic responds because a narrow lead claim only ever reached the smaller slice.

signal.check: The headline leads with a niche benefit that only a small slice of the target segment cares about, while a wider benefit sits buried in the body.

expected_effect.size: one claim over another in a headline moved results up to 10 times in one keyed test, per source

risk.note: A headline choice.

prerequisites: The segment picked in R16
steps: List the claims the product can make for the chosen segment.
Estimate which claim would move the widest share of that segment, not the whole store.
Put that claim in the headline; move narrower claims into the body or a minority of variants.
Never let a narrow claim in the headline crowd out the wider one.

test.method: Run the wide-claim headline against the narrow-claim headline as 2 variants.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend to compare.

title: Default the appeal to cure and reward over prevention
hypothesis: If the appeal is framed as a cure or a reward rather than prevention of a bad outcome, then response rises because positive, reward-framed appeals outpulled prevention-framed ones in cited keyed tests.
does_not_apply_when: Categories that genuinely sell on risk or security, where no store case is shown in this playbook

signal.check: The draft frames the product mainly as avoiding a bad outcome (decay, embarrassment, loss) rather than the reward it delivers.

expected_effect.size: positive framing outpulled negative 4 to 1 in one set of keyed print tests

risk.note: A framing choice.

steps: Identify the prevention-framed version of the appeal (avoiding decay, embarrassment, loss).
Rewrite it as the reward or cure the product actually delivers.
Never picture the afflicted state or show the 'before' as the centerpiece.

test.method: Run a cure or reward framed variant against a prevention framed variant.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend or sends to compare.

title: Match story depth to awareness stage: more story early, offer only for the most-aware
hypothesis: If pages and emails give more story to problem-aware and solution-aware readers, a short story plus testimonials to product-aware readers, and just the offer to the most-aware, then each reader gets only the argument they still need.

signal.check: The same long story or the same offer-only copy runs to both a cold audience and a warm, product-aware audience.

risk.note: A structure choice per audience.

prerequisites: Awareness stage identified for the traffic (R16)
steps: For problem-aware or solution-aware traffic, write a medium to long story that builds the case.
For product-aware traffic, write a short story plus several testimonials.
For most-aware traffic (past buyers, warm list), skip the story and lead with the offer.

test.method: Send the stage-matched version to its matching audience and a mismatched version to the same audience as a control.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Create contrast with the old way or category, never attack a named rival
hypothesis: If copy contrasts the product with the old way of doing things instead of naming and attacking a competitor, then it persuades without legal or platform risk because attacking a rival by name reads as unfair and can violate ad policy.

signal.check: A draft names a specific competitor to attack, or uses lines like 'avoid imitations' aimed at a rival.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source notes attacking a rival directly is 'never good advertising'

risk.note: Naming a rival risks a policy strike or a legal complaint; contrast with the category instead.

prerequisites: The real rival identified in R15
steps: Identify the old way, habit, or category norm the product replaces.
Write the contrast against that old way, never against a named brand.
If a comparison chart is used, verify facts on both sides and keep it about the category, not one named rival.

test.method: Check the final draft for any named competitor or attack line before it ships.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Name the true, ownable difference and check no rival could sign the line
hypothesis: If the copy names the specific feature that makes the product different, explains why it works, and passes a check that no competitor could sign the same line, then the claim resists price comparison because a generic benefit any rival could also claim carries no weight.

signal.check: The unique selling point in the draft is a claim most competitors could also make (quality, fast shipping, great service) with no named mechanism behind it.

risk.note: A claim must be true, or the brand must make it true, before it ships.

prerequisites: Verified product facts from the brand record
steps: Name the specific feature or mechanism that makes the product different.
Explain in one line why it works and why alternatives fail, using only verified facts.
Paste the line onto a rival's page in your head; if it would still be true for them, keep digging for a brand-only fact.
Confirm the claim traces to the brand record before it ships.

test.method: Ask someone to guess if the claim could belong to a competitor; rewrite until they say no.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Build one reusable copy skeleton per product line for a catalogue brand
hypothesis: If a brand with many SKUs builds one reusable headline formula, bullet order and proof slot per product line, then copy output speeds up because each SKU is filled into a proven skeleton instead of rewritten from scratch, while the spec and image stay SKU-specific.
does_not_apply_when: A hero-SKU brand with only a handful of products

signal.check: Each new SKU's copy is written from a blank page with no shared headline formula, bullet order or proof slot reused from the product line.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A template; keep the SKU-specific spec and image unique so ads do not read as identical.

prerequisites: A product line with more than a handful of SKUs and a filled feature-and-benefit table
steps: Write one headline formula that fits every SKU in the product line.
Fix the bullet order every SKU's copy will follow.
Fix the slot where proof (rating, review count, or spec) goes for every SKU.
Fill in the SKU-specific spec, price and image for each product without changing the skeleton.
Verify the skeleton against real brand data before wide use.

test.method: Time how long the next 5 SKUs take to copy with the skeleton versus the last 5 without it.
test.read_point: After the next 5 SKUs are copied.

title: Reuse one headline promise across the ad, the PDP first line and the collection hero
hypothesis: If the same headline promise appears on the ad, the PDP's first line and the collection hero, then the visitor's journey feels consistent because the promise that got the click is the promise that greets them on arrival.

signal.check: The ad's headline promise does not appear anywhere on the landing page or PDP the ad points to.

risk.note: A wording consistency step.

prerequisites: The landing page or PDP the ad points to
steps: Write the headline's biggest benefit once.
Reuse that same promise, in the same words or close to it, as the PDP or hero's first line.
Check this against the exception: a feature lead may beat it for a spec-comparing buyer (see the feature-lead idea).

test.method: Click the ad and check the landing page's first line repeats the headline promise.
test.read_point: Before the ad set ships and again after launch.

title: Make sure a reader who sees only the headline can say what's sold and for whom
hypothesis: If every headline passes the test of being shown alone, and a reader can still say what is sold and for whom, then fewer wrong-fit clicks and confused visitors occur because blind or clever headlines pull the wrong readers even while raising clicks.

signal.check: A headline reads as a pun, riddle or curiosity line with no product or benefit named in it.

risk.note: A headline check.

steps: Show the headline alone, with no image or body copy.
Ask: can a stranger say what is sold and who it is for?
If not, rewrite with the product, the benefit, and who it is for, and drop any blind, clever or punny wording.

test.method: Show the headline alone to someone unfamiliar with the brief and ask them to describe what is sold.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Put a true specific in the headline: a number, time, count or price
hypothesis: If the headline carries a true, checkable number, time, count or price instead of a generic superlative, then it earns more belief because specific claims are either checkably true or a lie, while generalities get discounted.
does_not_apply_when: No true figure exists yet in the brand record for this claim

signal.check: The headline uses a vague word ('best', 'fast', 'premium') where a real number, time or price exists in the brand record and is not being used.

risk.note: The specific must be verified true before it ships.

prerequisites: A verified number, time, count or price from the brand record
steps: Find a true number, time, count or price relevant to the headline's claim.
Swap the vague word for that specific.
Verify the specific against the brand record before shipping.

test.method: Run the specific-number headline against a superlative version of the same claim.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend to compare, judged with cost per purchase as the real measure.

title: Prefer the shorter of two equally good headlines, and flag any over 12 words
hypothesis: If two headlines carry the same benefit and specific, the shorter one is chosen, and headlines over 12 words are flagged for a cut, then more of the target reads it fully because cited readership data shows longer headlines lose readers.

signal.check: A candidate headline runs over 12 words without adding a benefit or a specific beyond a shorter version.

expected_effect.size: 3-word headlines were fully read by 87.3 percent versus 77.9 percent for 13-plus words, in a 1939-40 print readership study

risk.note: Never shorten by cutting the benefit or the specific.

steps: Count words in each headline candidate.
Where two headlines carry the same benefit and specific, keep the shorter one.
Flag any headline over 12 words and try to cut filler, not the benefit or specific.

test.method: Run a shortened headline against the original longer version as 2 variants.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend to compare, with cost per purchase as the deciding measure.

title: Write a headline bank of at least 10 candidates before choosing 3
hypothesis: If the writer drafts at least 10 headline candidates before narrowing to 3, then the final choice is stronger because a headline change alone has swung returns 5 to 10 times in keyed print tests.

signal.check: Fewer than 10 headline candidates were written before the final 3 were chosen for the ad set.

expected_effect.size: a headline change alone swung keyed print results 5 to 10 times in one source's account

risk.note: Time cost only.

prerequisites: The buying question and appeal from R19-R20
steps: Write at least 10 headline candidates using different generators (Caples' 4 qualities, a specific-number version, a contrast version, a feature-led version).
Run the 3-question test on each and cut any that fail.
Rank the survivors and mark the top 3 with different angles.
When a launched ad fails, change its headline first before touching price or offer.

test.method: Track how many headline candidates were written versus shipped, and compare cost per purchase against a set with fewer candidates.
test.read_point: After the ad set reaches enough spend to compare.

title: Use Caples' 4 headline qualities as generators, not fixed templates
hypothesis: If the headline bank includes one version for each of self-interest, news, curiosity, and quick easy way, then the bank covers more real angles because each quality pulls a genuinely different type of reader response.

signal.check: The headline bank has several headlines that are all the same quality (all curiosity, or all self-interest) with no coverage of the other 3.

risk.note: A generation technique, not a claim risk.

prerequisites: The one idea and appeal chosen in P2
steps: Write one headline for self-interest (what's in it for the reader).
Write one for news (something new about the product or offer).
Write one for curiosity (with a payoff that matches, per R32).
Write one for a quick, easy way to get the result.

test.method: Check the final bank has at least one headline per quality before ranking the top 3.
test.read_point: Before the headline bank is finalised.

title: Use curiosity hooks only when targeting and the payoff match
hypothesis: If curiosity is used only where the targeting is tight and the body pays off the exact tease, then the ad avoids pulling the wrong audience because a mismatched curiosity hook, like sex over patio furniture, attracts eyeballs that never convert.

signal.check: A curiosity or mystery hook in the ad has no clear connection to the product or the targeting, or the body never pays off the tease for the intended buyer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; mismatched mystery ads raised CTR about 18 percent while lowering purchases in one uncited study

risk.note: A mismatched curiosity hook can raise CTR while hurting conversion and, if spammy, risk the ad account.

prerequisites: Tight targeting for the intended buyer
steps: Check the curiosity hook is relevant to the exact targeted audience, not a broad or clickbait tease.
Confirm the body copy pays off the tease clearly for that audience.
Cut any curiosity line that could pull an unrelated audience.

test.method: Compare CTR against cost per purchase for the curiosity variant; a high CTR with a high cost per purchase signals a mismatch.
test.read_point: After the variant reaches enough spend to compare CTR and cost per purchase.

title: Test the headline beside the real image before shipping
hypothesis: If the headline is mocked up beside the actual product image on a phone before shipping, then fewer ads confuse the viewer because a headline that reads fine alone can fail beside a mismatched or busy image.

signal.check: The headline is finalised in a document without ever being placed next to the actual image or video brief on a phone-width mock-up.

risk.note: A pre-launch check.

prerequisites: The final image or video brief
steps: Mock up the top 3 headlines beside the real image on a phone-width preview.
Count 2 seconds and check the ad is understood in that time.
Compare the mock-up among 5 to 10 other ads to judge it in context, not alone.
Rewrite or ask for an image change if the headline needs the body to make sense.

test.method: Show the mocked-up ad for 2 seconds to someone unfamiliar with the brief and ask what it sells.
test.read_point: Before the ad set ships.

title: Give every ad enough product identity to stand alone; skip the product name in a long-form hero
hypothesis: If ads and product pages always name the product while a long-form sales page hero leads with the reader's problem instead, then each surface fits its job because an ad must stand alone but a sales page hero converts better by opening on the reader, not the brand.
does_not_apply_when: A household-name brand, where the product name can lead any hero

signal.check: An ad has no clear product identity and could be for anything, or a long-form sales page hero opens with the product name instead of the reader's problem.

risk.note: A structure choice by surface.

steps: For any ad, confirm the product identity is clear enough that the ad could not be for a different product.
For a product page, keep the product name as the title (H1).
For a long-form sales page hero, lead with the reader's problem or goal and name the product only after the promise, unless the brand is a household name.

test.method: Cover the image and check if a reader can still say what the ad sells; check the sales page hero's first line for a reader problem versus a brand name.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Check every hook for promise, intrigue and emotion, none spammy or clickbait
hypothesis: If every hook is checked for a promise that is not spammy, intrigue that is not confusing, and emotion that is not clickbait, then fewer hooks get flagged or ignored because a spammy promise can push email to spam and a clickbait hook can risk the ad account.

signal.check: A hook reads as spammy ('You won't believe'), confusing, or clickbait with no real payoff behind it.

risk.note: A spammy hook can hurt deliverability or risk the ad account, not just conversion.

steps: Read the hook and check it makes a real promise, not a spammy line.
Check the intrigue is clear, not confusing.
Check the emotion is earned by the product, not manufactured clickbait.
Cut or rewrite the hook if it fails any of the 3 checks.

test.method: Run the checked hook against the original in 2 variants and compare hook rate and cost per purchase.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend to compare.

title: Cut the lead: keep the first sentence to 14 words or fewer, ideally 7 to 10
hypothesis: If the first line's only job is to get the second line read, and it stays at 14 words or fewer, then more readers keep going because a long or throat-clearing lead loses the reader before the pitch starts.

signal.check: The first sentence runs over 14 words, opens with a greeting, 'I hope', or 'what if I told you', or takes more than 1 line to say something.

expected_effect.size: unknown; heuristic target of 7 to 10 words, 14 at most

risk.note: A cut, not a claim.

steps: Read the current first line and count its words.
Cut any greeting, 'I hope this finds you well', or 'what if I told you' opener.
Rewrite the first line to state the payoff in 14 words or fewer, aiming for 7 to 10.

test.method: Run the shortened first line against the original as 2 variants.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend or sends to compare.

title: Default cold hooks to a confident declarative, not a hedged question
hypothesis: If cold feed hooks default to a confident declarative sentence instead of a generic question, then more of the audience keeps watching or reading because a study across 3 creator channels found winners state things while losers ask questions.

signal.check: The hook opens with a hedged, generic question ('Want to save money?') instead of a declarative statement of the payoff.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 run across 3 organic creator channels found declaratives beat questions

risk.note: Needs brand data to confirm on paid ads; the source's demo is organic video.

steps: Rewrite the hook's question into a declarative statement of the payoff.
If a question is kept, make sure it names the buyer's exact situation, never a generic hedge.
Test a declarative and a precise-question variant against each other.

test.method: Run a declarative-hook variant against a question-hook variant on the same audience.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend to compare.

title: State the claim, then amplify with a comparison or contrast in the next line
hypothesis: If sentence 1 states the claim and sentence 2 adds a comparison or contrast, then the hook holds attention longer because winning hooks in a cross-channel study pair a stat with a second-sentence amplifier while losers state and stop.

signal.check: The hook's second sentence repeats the first instead of adding a comparison, contrast, or untold fact.

risk.note: A structural tweak.

steps: Write the claim in sentence 1.
Write sentence 2 as a comparison, contrast, or an untold fact that amplifies sentence 1.
Check sentence 2 does not just restate sentence 1 in different words.

test.method: Run the amplified 2-line hook against a version that just restates the claim twice.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend or sends to compare.

title: Bridge the headline to the body with one flowing lead-in device
hypothesis: If the body opens with one device that continues the headline's thought (a question, an authority quote, a free taste, a challenge, a story), then the reader keeps moving because the jump from headline to body does not feel abrupt.

signal.check: The body's first line has no clear connection to the headline; it jumps to a new topic or a generic opener.

risk.note: A transition choice.

prerequisites: A finished headline
steps: Pick one lead-in device: continue the thought, ask a question, quote an authority, give a free taste, challenge the reader, or tell a short story.
Write the body's first line using that device so it flows directly from the headline.
Check the connection reads naturally when the headline and first line are read together.

test.method: Read the headline and first body line together and check for a natural flow versus an abrupt jump.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Hint the mechanism in the hook; never withhold everything until the click
hypothesis: If the hook gives a real hint of how the product works instead of saying only 'click to learn how', then click-to-purchase rate rises because withholding everything raised clicks and lowered buyers in a cited comparison.

signal.check: The hook or email teases a benefit with zero mechanism hint, using lines like 'click to find out' with nothing else.

expected_effect.size: unknown; withholding everything raised clicks and lowered buyers in a cited comparison

risk.note: A hint, not the full reveal; keep the punchline for the end.

steps: Identify the one real mechanism or reason the product works.
Add a 1-line hint of that mechanism to the hook or subject line.
Keep the full explanation and the CTA behind the click, but never zero hint.

test.method: Compare click-to-purchase rate between a zero-hint tease and a mechanism-hint version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable sends or spend.

title: Challenge a common belief only when the product can honestly justify it
hypothesis: If a contrarian or belief-challenging hook is used only when the product truly justifies the challenge, then trust holds because a challenge the product cannot back up reads as a gimmick once the reader clicks through.

signal.check: A hook challenges a common belief (a CJN or contrarian format) with no real product fact that justifies the challenge.

risk.note: An unjustified challenge can burn trust with an interested reader who clicks through and finds no backing.

prerequisites: A verified product fact that supports the challenge
steps: Before writing a challenge hook, name the belief being challenged in the reader's words.
Check the brand record for a real fact that justifies the challenge.
If no such fact exists, drop the challenge format and use a straightforward claim instead.
Never write 'truth is beside the point'; every challenge must be true.

test.method: Check the click-through content actually delivers on the challenge made in the hook.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Ground AI-generated hooks in the brand's own winning ads before use
hypothesis: If an LLM's hook drafts are checked against the brand's own top-performing ads and stripped of any invented proof, then the hooks fit the brand and stay compliant because a model left ungrounded writes generic hooks and can invent fake proof like a fabricated study count.

signal.check: An AI tool is used to draft hooks with a generic prompt and no reference to the brand's own past ad results, or its output includes an invented statistic or credential.

risk.note: An AI-invented proof line (a fake study count, a fake credential) must never ship; it is a compliance risk.

prerequisites: Past ad copy with results for the brand
steps: Write hooks by hand first, before asking the model for any drafts.
Give the model the brand's own winning ad copy as reference, not a cold prompt.
Only lift AI-suggested lines that beat the hand-written version.
Strip any statistic, credential, or count the model added; verify every fact before it ships.
Have a human pick the final hook for voice fit.

test.method: Compare AI-assisted, brand-grounded hooks against hand-written hooks on the same audience.
test.read_point: After each set reaches enough spend to compare.

title: Structure ad body as attention, interest, desire, proof, then action
hypothesis: If the ad body follows attention, interest, desire, proof, then action, closing proof with a store-owned signal rather than a generic quality claim, then the ad argues more completely because the sequence covers the buyer's full decision path before the ask.

signal.check: The ad body jumps from a claim straight to the CTA with no distinct proof step, or its proof step is a generic quality line instead of a store-owned signal.

risk.note: A structure choice.

steps: Write the attention line (the hook).
Add an interest line that gives a reason to keep reading.
Build desire with a benefit tied to a feature.
Close the proof step with a store-owned signal: a star rating, a review count, or a return-policy line, not a generic quality claim.
End with one clear CTA.

test.method: Check the finished ad has a distinct, store-owned proof line before the CTA.
test.read_point: Before the ad ships.

title: Give the ad body one situation, one feature, one benefit, not a component list
hypothesis: If the ad body picks one recognisable situation, one relevant feature, and the practical benefit that feature delivers, instead of listing components, then the ad reads more clearly because a stacked list of specs reads as noise while one connected chain reads as an argument.

signal.check: The ad body lists multiple product components or specs in a row with no single connected situation-feature-benefit chain.

risk.note: A structure choice; do not repeat the same component list in every ad variant.

prerequisites: The feature-and-benefit table
steps: Pick 1 recognisable situation the target buyer is in.
Pick 1 relevant feature that addresses that situation.
Write the practical benefit that feature credibly provides.
Cut any additional feature or spec that is not part of this one chain.

test.method: Check each ad variant uses a different situation-feature-benefit chain, not the same component list reworded.
test.read_point: Before the ad set ships.

title: Pick the email structure before writing: PPAS, CJN, HSO or the outline block
hypothesis: If the writer picks a named structure (PPAS for a promo, CJN for a justified belief shift, HSO for a story, or the outline block for anything) before drafting, then the email holds together because the parts fall into a proven order instead of a freeform draft.

signal.check: An email is drafted freeform with no named structure chosen first, and the sections do not follow a clear order.

risk.note: A structural choice, not a claim.

prerequisites: The email's single goal (value or sell)
steps: For a promo email, use PPAS: problem, promise, agitate, solution, never agitate before the promise.
For a justified belief shift, use CJN with a real justification.
For a story, use HSO: hook, story with 2 beats, lesson, offer.
For anything else, use the outline block: goal, subject, preview, story, content, CTA, P.S.

test.method: Check the finished email follows its chosen structure's order before it sends.
test.read_point: Before the send, then compare against past sends with no fixed structure.

title: Tell a story with a turn and a lesson at the end, not a timeline
hypothesis: If a story email has a main character, a goal, adversity, a turn, and the lesson placed at the end, then it holds attention because a chronology with the lesson stated up front loses the reason to keep reading.

signal.check: A story email or founder story block lists events in order with the lesson given away in the first line, instead of building to a turn.

risk.note: A structural rewrite.

steps: Name the main character, their goal, and the adversity they hit.
Find the turn: the moment things changed.
Relive that one moment instead of retelling the whole timeline.
Place the lesson at the end, after the turn, then loop to the reader's own next problem before the CTA.

test.method: Check the draft has adversity and a turn before the lesson, not a chronology with the lesson stated first.
test.read_point: Before the send.

title: Build the page in a fixed order: hero, blocks, CTA every 2 to 3 sections, FAQ last
hypothesis: If the page follows hero, blocks that each serve the one idea, a CTA every 2 to 3 sections, and FAQ at the bottom, then more readers convert because the header-only read tells the full story and no one has to hunt for the next step.

signal.check: Reading only the page's headers does not tell the story from problem to offer, or the FAQ sits above the fold instead of at the bottom.

risk.note: A layout-of-words choice; page build itself is 07-LPG's.

prerequisites: The hero copy from R104 and the awareness stage from R23
steps: Write the hero: eyebrow, headline, deck, one CTA, answering who this is for, why keep reading, what to do next.
Order the blocks: what it is and why, relate to the reader, feature-and-benefit bullets, testimonials each answering an objection, price positioning, guarantee, urgency if real, FAQ last.
Place a CTA or price block every 2 to 3 sections.
Read only the headers in order and check they tell the story alone.
End with a P.S. or a final restated offer.

test.method: Read only the page's headers in order and check a stranger can follow the argument to the offer.
test.read_point: Before the page ships.

title: Give the reader every proven claim needed to decide, all serving the one idea, no padding
hypothesis: If a page or long email includes every proven claim the reader needs to decide, with each claim serving the one idea and nothing padded in, then interested readers convert more because omitting a needed claim loses the readers who needed exactly that fact, while padding wastes their attention.

signal.check: The page or email is missing a claim an interested reader would need, or it repeats filler points that do not serve the one idea.

risk.note: Length follows the product and the reader's interest, not a fixed word count.

prerequisites: The one idea from P2 and the claim list from the feature-and-benefit table
steps: List every proven claim relevant to the reader's decision.
Check each claim is a sub-point of the one idea; cut any that pulls toward a second idea.
For a cold feed ad, put the whole argument before the truncation point; save the full case for the page or email.
Overwrite first, then cut, rather than padding to hit a length.

test.method: List every claim the shipped copy makes and check none is missing that an interested reader would want, and none is filler.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Pace copy: mix short and long lines, keep paragraphs short
hypothesis: If copy mixes short and long lines with a short scroll-stopper line where a skimmer's eye should stop, then more of the reader gets through the copy because a wall of same-length lines reads as harder work and a skimmer disengages.

signal.check: The draft is a wall of same-length lines, or every line is a one-liner with no variation.

risk.note: A pacing pass.

steps: Read the draft for line-length variation; mix short and long lines like an action movie, not a wall of long lines or all one-liners.
Add a short, bold scroll-stopper line where a skimmer's eye should land.
Keep paragraphs to 1 to 3 sentences in feed ads.

test.method: Scroll through the draft without reading closely and check the offer still rebuilds from the bold and short lines.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Show many benefits as short bullets, not long sentences
hypothesis: If page and long-email benefits are broken into short bullets instead of long sentences, then more of them get read because bullets are the fastest reading unit and a long bullet defeats the purpose.

signal.check: A page or email buries several benefits inside a long paragraph instead of a short bullet list.

risk.note: A formatting pass.

steps: Find benefits currently buried in long paragraphs.
Break them into short bullets, one benefit per line.
Cut any bullet that runs long enough to defeat the purpose; shorten or split it.
Do not centre small bullet text; keep it left-aligned.

test.method: Compare read-through completion or scroll depth before and after converting paragraphs to bullets.
test.read_point: After the page or email runs with the bullet format.

title: Restate the main benefit from several angles in long copy
hypothesis: If long copy restates the main benefit from several angles (how they'll feel, how others see them, safety, savings) broken up by selling subheads, then the argument sticks better because a single statement of the benefit fades while multiple angles reinforce it.

signal.check: A long page or sales email states the main benefit once and never returns to it from a different angle.

risk.note: Length follows the product; do not restate for a short feed ad.

prerequisites: Long-form copy (a page or sales email)
steps: Identify the main benefit already stated once.
Add 2 to 3 more angles: how the buyer will feel, how others will see them, the safety it provides, the money it saves.
Break each restatement with a selling subhead or caption so it reads as new, not repetitive.

test.method: Check the finished long-form copy restates the main benefit from at least 2 different angles.
test.read_point: Before the page or email ships.

title: Write cold ads for strangers, list emails for people who already know the product
hypothesis: If cold acquisition ads explain the product while list emails skip straight to 'do these work, how, why these', then warm subscribers stop feeling talked down to because a returning buyer already knows what the product is.

signal.check: An email to the store's own list opens by explaining what the product is, as if to a first-time visitor.

risk.note: A copy-audience match.

prerequisites: Knowledge of whether the send goes to cold traffic or the owned list
steps: Check whether the asset targets cold traffic or the brand's own list.
For cold ads, keep enough explanation of what the product is.
For list emails, cut the 'what is this' framing and open with do these work, how, and why these rather than others.

test.method: Compare click and reply rates on a list-aware email against a version that re-explains the product.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable list sends.

title: Write product pages in 3 blocks: title, benefit bullets, spec block
hypothesis: If a product page has a title naming the product and its key spec, a bullet block tying each feature to a benefit, and a spec block with exact numbers, then shoppers decide faster because they can filter and compare without hunting through prose.

signal.check: The product page's title has no key spec, its bullets list features with no benefit, or exact numbers a shopper would filter by are missing.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: Page layout and build stay with 07-LPG; this covers the words only.

prerequisites: The feature-and-benefit table and exact product specs from the brand record
steps: Write a title that names the product and its key spec.
Write a bullet block where each bullet ties a specific feature to a benefit.
Write a spec block with the exact numbers a shopper filters or searches by.
Add a note on who the product does not fit, where a real non-fit exists.
Check every number traces to the brand record.

test.method: Check the page against the 3-block structure and confirm every spec number traces to the brand record.
test.read_point: Before the page ships, then after a comparable traffic window.

title: Ladder every feature to a benefit using the product's own spec units
hypothesis: If every feature is laddered to a buyer benefit using the product's own units (denier, GSM, mAh, wash count) instead of a marketing adjective, then claims feel more credible because a unit a shopper recognises reads as fact while an adjective reads as opinion.

signal.check: A feature is described with a marketing adjective ('durable', 'powerful') instead of the product's own spec unit.

risk.note: The benefit must not become a number the product data cannot support.

prerequisites: The feature-and-benefit table with exact spec units
steps: For each feature, react 'BIG DEAL, what's in it for me?' and answer 'You benefit by...'
Keep asking 'what's the benefit of that?' until reaching the end value.
Use the product's own spec unit (denier, GSM, mAh, wash count) instead of a vague adjective.
Check the final benefit did not overstate what the spec actually supports.

test.method: Scan the draft for any adjective that could be replaced by a spec unit from the brand record.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Choose feature-lead or benefit-lead by audience, always pair the two
hypothesis: If the lead is a benefit by default but switches to a feature lead when the buyer compares specs or came for one named feature, and every lead is paired with its other half, then the copy fits how that buyer actually decides because a feature headline has beaten a benefit headline for spec-comparing shoppers.

signal.check: The lead is always a soft benefit even when the brief says the buyer compares specs or distrusts soft language, or a feature is stated with no paired benefit.

expected_effect.size: a feature headline beat a benefit headline in one cited case

risk.note: A lead choice, not a claim risk.

steps: Check the brief: does this buyer compare specs, distrust soft language, or came for one feature they heard about?
If yes, lead with the feature; otherwise lead with the benefit.
Pair whichever leads with its other half: every feature gets a benefit, every benefit gets a supporting feature.

test.method: Run a feature-led and a benefit-led variant of the same ad against each other.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches enough spend to compare.

title: Swap every vague quality word for a concrete, checkable detail
hypothesis: If a vague word is zoomed in one step at a time until it becomes an object, person, place or action, then the line becomes more believable because concrete words are things a reader can picture, while abstract words like 'regain fitness' carry no image.

signal.check: The draft has a vague quality word ('a better way', 'seamless', 'premium feel') with no concrete detail beneath it.

risk.note: A rewrite pass.

steps: Find each vague or abstract phrase in the draft.
Rewrite it one step more concrete at a time until it names an object, person, place or action.
Run a sensory pass where it fits: what it looks, sounds, feels, smells or tastes like, skipping senses that do not apply.

test.method: Circle every adjective in the draft and check each now points to something the reader could drop on their foot.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Pass every figurative headline line through the reasonable-reader test
hypothesis: If a figurative line in a headline is used only where no reasonable reader would take it as a literal spec, time, count or outcome, then the brand avoids a false-claim problem because a figurative line taken literally reads as a broken promise.

signal.check: A headline uses a figurative phrase ('a thousand uses in one box') that a reasonable reader could take as a literal number, time, or outcome.

risk.note: Never use figurative language on a number, time, outcome or safety claim.

steps: Find every figurative or metaphorical line in the headline.
Ask: would a reasonable reader take this as a literal spec, count, time or outcome?
If yes, rewrite it as a plain, literal claim instead.

test.method: Show the headline to someone unfamiliar with the product and ask what number or fact they think it states.
test.read_point: Before the headline ships.

title: Cut any spec bullet that answers no real filter or search a shopper uses
hypothesis: If every spec bullet is checked against whether a shopper would actually search or filter by it, then the copy reads tighter because a bullet that answers no real question is noise the reader has to skip past.

signal.check: A bullet block includes a spec that answers no size guide, filter, or 'will this work for me' question a real shopper asks.

risk.note: A cutting pass on the spec list.

prerequisites: The relevant angle for the ad or page
steps: List every spec bullet currently in the copy.
For each, ask if a shopper would search or filter by it.
Cut any bullet that answers no such question and is not the one fact this angle needs.

test.method: Check the trimmed bullet list against actual search or filter terms shoppers use on the site.
test.read_point: Before the page ships.

title: Describe a big commitment by what changes, not its scary label
hypothesis: If a costly or effortful offer is described by what actually changes for the buyer instead of by its intimidating label, then it feels more approachable because a label like '12-week program' sounds like a bigger ask than the plain description of what happens.

signal.check: A big commitment (a long program, a subscription, a high-touch service) is described by its scary-sounding label rather than by what the buyer actually experiences.

risk.note: A reframe, not a new claim.

steps: Identify the label that makes the commitment sound bigger than it feels day to day.
Describe instead what actually changes: what the buyer does, sees, or experiences.
Check the description still matches the real terms.

test.method: Run the label-led version against the what-changes version on the same offer.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Word a bundle or kit as one line: what's included, the real saving, and why it works together
hypothesis: If a bundle or kit is worded as one line naming what is included, the saving versus buying separately, and the reason the pieces work together, then shoppers understand the value faster because the math is done for them instead of left implied.

signal.check: A bundle or kit's copy names the price but not what is included, the real saving, or why the pieces belong together.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: Compute the saving in code from real prices, never in the model.

prerequisites: Real component prices for each item in the bundle
steps: List what is included in the bundle in one line.
Compute the real saving versus buying the items separately, in code.
State the one reason the pieces work better together than alone.

test.method: Check the saving figure against a manual calculation of the real component prices.
test.read_point: Before the bundle copy ships.

title: Replace every superlative with a number, a name or a checkable fact
hypothesis: If every superlative and vague adjective is replaced with a checkable number, name or process fact, then belief rises because a specific claim is either true or a lie, while a generality gets discounted by the reader.

signal.check: The draft uses 'best', 'quality', 'premium' or another superlative with no number, name or fact behind it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 6 of 9 sources in this playbook independently back this rule

risk.note: The replacement fact must be verified before it ships.

prerequisites: Verified facts from the brand record
steps: Scan the draft for every superlative or vague adjective.
Find a checkable number, name, or process fact to replace each one.
Verify each replacement fact against the brand record before shipping.

test.method: Circle every remaining adjective in the final draft and confirm each is either specific or removed.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Run the 3-question test on every line: can you visualise it, falsify it, and can no one else say it
hypothesis: If every sentence of an ad, hook or hero line is checked against 3 questions, and rewritten on 3 no answers, then the copy earns more belief because a line that fails all 3 checks is unpicturable, unfalsifiable and could belong to any competitor.

signal.check: A key line in the draft cannot be pictured, cannot be checked true or false, or a competitor could say the exact same thing.

risk.note: A line-level QA check.

steps: For each key line, ask: can I visualise it?
Ask: can I falsify it (prove it true or false)?
Ask: could nobody else say this?
If the line gets 3 no answers, rewrite it before shipping.

test.method: Score every key line 3-for-3, 2-for-3 or worse and rewrite anything below 2.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Rank proof by strength: demonstration first, then third-party evidence, then cost narration, then analogy
hypothesis: If proof is chosen in order of strength (a demonstration first, then evidence not created by the brand, then cost narration or process facts, then analogy last), then claims land harder because a bare, unranked claim reads as unsupported no matter how true it is.

signal.check: A result claim has no proof at all, or only the weakest type (an analogy) when stronger proof (a demonstration or a third-party review) is available.

risk.note: Any statistic or quote used as proof must come from a checked source in the brand record, never invented.

prerequisites: Access to reviews, demonstrations, or process facts
steps: Check if a real demonstration (a video, a before-after, a side-by-side) is available; use it first.
If not, use evidence not created by the brand: a testimonial, a review, a third-party test.
If neither exists, use cost narration or a process fact.
Use analogy only as a last resort, and never let it stand in for real proof of a specific outcome.

test.method: Check the proof type used against the ranking and swap up a level if a stronger type is available.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Show conviction with real proof instead of just telling the reader the claim
hypothesis: If a result claim is shown through a real before-and-after case or a packaging shot doing the proving, instead of a caption asserting quality, then belief rises because 'here's how mine went from this to this' beats 'you can lose 20 lb' in a cited heuristic 90 percent of the time.

signal.check: A results claim is asserted in a caption or headline with no shown case, image, or demonstration behind it.

expected_effect.size: showing beats telling about 90 percent of the time, per one source's heuristic

risk.note: Any shown case must be real and verifiable.

prerequisites: A real before-and-after case, a packaging shot, or a demonstration
steps: Find the claim currently only asserted, not shown.
Replace it with a real case: an actual before-and-after, a named customer's result, or a packaging or unboxing shot doing the showing.
Verify the shown case is real and not staged or invented.

test.method: Run the shown-proof version against the asserted-claim version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable spend or sends.

title: Quote the brand's real star rating and review count as proof
hypothesis: If copy quotes the real star rating and review count from the brand's own review platform instead of one hand-picked testimonial, then proof feels stronger because volume signals strength to a skimming reader.
does_not_apply_when: No review platform or rating exists yet for the product

signal.check: The brand has a real star rating and review count on its platform, but the ad or page only shows a single hand-picked quote.

risk.note: Check current endorsement and review rules for the market before use.

prerequisites: A live review platform with a real rating and count
steps: Pull the current star rating and review count from the brand's platform.
Add it as a proof line near the CTA, alongside or instead of a single quote.
Check the figure against the platform before every use so it stays current.

test.method: Run a version with the star rating and count against a version with only a hand-picked quote.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable spend or sends.

title: Keep claims small and believable; back any near-unbelievable claim with an example
hypothesis: If a claim stays small and attainable, and any claim close to unbelievable is backed with a real example on the same surface, then trust holds because a believed small claim beats a doubted big one, and an impossible claim never runs at all.

signal.check: The draft has a big, round-number claim with no example beside it, or a claim that reads as impossible.

risk.note: An impossible claim never ships, no matter how it is worded.

steps: Check every promise in the draft against what the brand record can actually support.
Shrink any claim that overreaches to a size the record backs.
Add a concrete example beside any claim a stranger would still doubt.
Cut any claim that is simply impossible.

test.method: Have someone unfamiliar with the brand read each claim and flag any they would not believe without an example.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Don't over-explain ordinary claims; save your defense for the bold ones
hypothesis: If ordinary, easily accepted claims are left unexplained while editing effort defends only the bold ones, then the copy reads tighter because readers accept ordinary statements without question and over-explaining them wastes their attention.

signal.check: The draft spends multiple sentences justifying an ordinary, easily believed claim while a genuinely bold claim gets no support at all.

risk.note: An editing-pass rule.

steps: Sort claims in the draft into ordinary and bold.
Cut extra justification sentences around ordinary claims.
Move that saved space into proof and examples for the bold claims.

test.method: Count sentences of justification per claim and check bold claims get more support than ordinary ones.
test.read_point: During the editing pass.

title: Name who the product does not fit, to build trust and cut returns
hypothesis: If copy names a real size, skin type, use case or climate the product does not fit, then trust rises and return rate falls because a stated non-fit reads as credibility and stops the wrong buyer from ordering in the first place.
does_not_apply_when: No real non-fit exists to name

signal.check: The product has a known real limit (a size range, a skin type, a climate, a use case) that never appears in the copy, and return rate for wrong-fit reasons is a known issue.

risk.note: Never invent a non-fit that isn't real; use only a true limit.

prerequisites: A real, known limit on who the product fits
steps: Check return data or product specs for a real size, skin type, use case, or climate limit.
Write a plain line naming who the product does not fit.
Place it near the spec block or FAQ, not buried at the very end.

test.method: Compare return rate for wrong-fit reasons before and after the non-fit line is added.
test.read_point: After a full return-window cycle post-launch.

title: Frame the offer as a service that takes the risk off the buyer
hypothesis: If the offer is framed as something the brand does for the buyer (a sample, a trial, goods to approve) rather than a demand to buy, then more buyers act because taking the risk onto the brand's side makes the ask easier to accept.

signal.check: The offer copy asks the buyer to take the risk (buy now, no easy way to try first) rather than offering to take the risk itself.

risk.note: The risk reversal must match what the brand's operations can honour.

prerequisites: A real guarantee or trial mechanism from the brand record
steps: Identify the store's real risk-reversal blockers: shipping cost, return hassle, sizing risk, effectiveness doubt.
Rewrite the offer to frame the brand as taking on that risk (a real guarantee, a real trial), not the buyer.
Confirm operations can honour the mechanism before it ships.

test.method: Run a risk-reversal-led offer against a plain buy-now offer.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: State the offer as one concrete line: what, the condition, and the scope
hypothesis: If the offer is stated in one line naming what is offered, the qualifying condition, and what it applies to, then fewer buyers hesitate at checkout because a vague offer leaves the buyer guessing whether they qualify.

signal.check: The offer is spread across several lines or vague about the condition or scope ('save big', 'special pricing for you').

risk.note: A wording clarity fix.

prerequisites: The exact offer terms from the brand record
steps: Write what is offered in plain words.
State the qualifying condition (minimum spend, a code, a date range).
State what it applies to (which products, first order only, or storewide).
Compress all 3 into one line.

test.method: Check the offer line answers what, condition and scope in one read.
test.read_point: Before the offer ships.

title: Write the strongest guarantee operations can actually honor, shown at the decision point
hypothesis: If the guarantee uses the longest, plainest term operations can honor and is shown next to the price and CTA, then buyers convert more because the risk-reversal is visible exactly when they are deciding.

signal.check: The guarantee is shorter than what operations could support, or it is written in fine print far from the price or the CTA.

expected_effect.size: a long guarantee (6 months to lifetime) is claimed to beat 30, 60 or 90 days for sales and returns, per one uncited source

risk.note: Never promise a term operations cannot actually deliver; check return rate and refund cost first.

prerequisites: Return rate, refund cost and margin data to confirm the term is affordable
steps: Check with operations for the longest guarantee term they can actually honor.
Write it in plain terms: length, what qualifies, how to claim.
Place it next to the price and the CTA, not buried in policy pages.
Match the wording exactly to the record's eligibility limits.

test.method: Run the longer, visible guarantee against the current shorter or buried one.
test.read_point: After a comparable traffic window for each version.

title: Use a deadline only when it's real; state the time or units left in digits
hypothesis: If a deadline is used only when it is real, stated in digits, and repeated with the CTA, then urgency drives action without legal or trust risk because a fake or vague countdown can break consumer law and burns trust when a reader notices.

signal.check: An ad or email uses urgency language ('selling fast', 'limited time') with no real end date, restock limit, or price change behind it.

risk.note: A fake or evergreen countdown can break consumer-protection law; remove urgency rather than soften a fake one.

prerequisites: A real, verified deadline, batch limit, or restock date
steps: Confirm a real date, batch, restock, or price change with a fact behind it.
State the time or units left in digits ('2 days left', '14 left in stock').
Give the reason for the deadline.
Repeat the CTA alongside the urgency line.
Set the copy to expire when the fact expires.

test.method: Check the deadline against the real underlying fact before every send, and confirm it expires on time.
test.read_point: Before the send or ad set ships, and again at the stated expiry.

title: Make believed value beat price with a real, computed value stack
