hypothesis: If the price is positioned against a value stack built from real component prices computed in code, rather than a cheapness appeal, then buyers see the price as reasonable because a stack shows what they are getting for what they pay instead of just asking them to trust a discount.

signal.check: The price appears with no value stack or comparison, or the stack uses estimated rather than real component prices.

risk.note: Every value in the stack must be a real price from the brand record; compute totals in code, never in the model.

prerequisites: Real prices for every component in the stack
steps: List every real component of what the buyer gets and its real price.
Compute the total value and the saving versus the asking price, in code.
Present the stack or the cost comparison against the real alternative before the CTA.
Never add a 'priceless' or invented-value line.

test.method: Run a value-stack version against a plain price-only version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Limit a special offer to a real group the buyer plausibly belongs to
hypothesis: If an offer is limited to a real group the buyer belongs to (veterans, members, past buyers, a profession) instead of a general discount, then response rises because a group-limited offer reads as earned rather than a blanket markdown, without ever faking the group.
does_not_apply_when: No real qualifying group exists for the brand's buyers

signal.check: The store runs only general storewide discounts with no group-limited offer, despite having a real identifiable group (past buyers, a loyalty tier, a profession segment).

risk.note: Never fake a qualifying group; the buyer must plausibly belong to it.

prerequisites: A real, identifiable buyer group
steps: Identify a real group the brand can honestly address (past buyers, a loyalty tier, a profession, a local area).
Word the offer as limited to that group.
Never extend the offer to people outside the real group under the same wording.

test.method: Run a group-limited offer against the same offer worded as general, to comparable audiences.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Offer a free trial on request rather than a part-price sample
hypothesis: If a trial or sample is offered free on request after the reader has engaged with the story, rather than at part-price or handed out unasked, then more requests convert to buyers because a requested free trial reads as earned interest while an unrequested giveaway cheapens the product.

signal.check: The brand runs a part-price sample offer, or hands out free product unasked, with no request step tied to the story.

expected_effect.size: unknown; cited historical cases favor free-on-request over part-price or unrequested giveaways

risk.note: Keep this as wording only; offer mechanics belong to 03-OFF.

prerequisites: A trial or sample mechanism the brand can support
steps: Write the trial offer as free, gated behind a request after reading the story, not automatic.
Avoid a part-price 'you pay for shipping, we cover the rest' framing where a fully free trial is affordable.
Never seed the product unasked and call it a trial offer.

test.method: Compare request rate and buy-through rate between a free-on-request trial and a part-price sample.
test.read_point: After each offer runs to comparable volume.

title: State the deeper reason to buy, not just the discount, on its own line
hypothesis: If the home page and the first line of a promo email state the deeper motivation to buy, separate from the discount, then the discount alone stops carrying the whole argument because a price cut is not itself a reason to want the product.

signal.check: A home page or promo email's first line is only the discount ('20% off today') with no separate line on why the buyer wants the product.

risk.note: A copy addition, not a pricing change.

prerequisites: The dominant appeal from R20
steps: Identify the deeper reason (the pain or motivation) behind wanting this product.
Write it as its own line, separate from the discount line.
Place the motivation line before or alongside the discount, not after it alone.

test.method: Run a version with a separate motivation line against a discount-only version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Word a promo code as one line: the percent, what it applies to, and how to get it
hypothesis: If a promo code beyond a flat storewide percent off is worded in one line with the amount, what it applies to, and how to get it, then fewer buyers abandon at checkout confused because the mechanism is stated plainly instead of assumed.

signal.check: A promo code offer states the discount but not what it applies to or exactly how to get the code (email gate, automatic, referral).

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source beyond one email-gate card, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A clarity fix at checkout.

prerequisites: The exact promo terms and how the code is delivered
steps: State the percent or amount off.
State what it applies to (all items, one category, first order only).
State how to get it: a code, an email-signup gate, or automatic at checkout.
Compress into one line near the CTA.

test.method: Check checkout abandonment for orders that entered a promo code before and after the one-line rewrite.
test.read_point: After a comparable order volume post-change.

title: Word subscription copy around the ongoing choice: what ships, how to pause, how to cancel, the saving
hypothesis: If subscription copy states what ships and when, how to pause or skip, how to cancel, and the saving versus a one-off order, then fewer subscribers feel trapped because the ongoing choice is made visible instead of hidden in fine print.

signal.check: Subscription copy sells only the first discount with no mention of the ship schedule, pause or skip option, or cancellation path.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: Clear cancel and pause terms reduce disputes and chargebacks even if they slightly lower first-order urgency.

prerequisites: The real subscription terms: ship schedule, pause and cancel process, saving vs one-off
steps: State what ships and how often.
State how to pause or skip a shipment.
State how to cancel in plain words.
State the real saving versus ordering one-off, computed from real prices.

test.method: Compare subscription churn and support tickets before and after adding the ongoing-choice wording.
test.read_point: After 2 to 3 billing cycles post-change.

title: State payment and delivery trust facts for a mobile-first, non-US market
hypothesis: If copy states cash-on-delivery availability, the price in local currency, and how order confirmation reaches the buyer, then more mobile-first shoppers in a market like India complete checkout because the exact payment and delivery facts they need to trust the order are answered up front.

signal.check: Checkout-adjacent copy is silent on cash-on-delivery availability, shows price with no clear local-currency framing, or does not say how order confirmation will reach the buyer (for example WhatsApp).

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: State only real, current payment and delivery facts.

prerequisites: Confirmed COD availability, currency display, and confirmation channel
steps: State whether cash on delivery is available and any condition on it.
Show the price clearly in the local currency.
State how order confirmation will reach the buyer (SMS, WhatsApp, email).

test.method: Compare checkout completion rate before and after adding the trust facts near checkout.
test.read_point: After a comparable order volume post-change.

title: Shift a belief in 6 steps, run against the store's real blockers
hypothesis: If an objection is treated as a belief and moved through 6 steps (name it, challenge gently, sympathise, show the old belief's failure, prove the new belief, sell from it), tied to the store's real blockers like shipping cost or sizing risk, then hesitant buyers convert more because the objection is handled with structure instead of a single rebuttal line.

signal.check: A known objection (shipping cost, return hassle, sizing risk, authenticity doubt) has no dedicated belief-shift copy anywhere in the funnel.

risk.note: Never tell the reader they are wrong; change the belief's focus or importance instead.

prerequisites: The store's real blockers, from tickets or checkout drop-off data
steps: Name the belief in the reader's own words.
Challenge it gently, without saying they are wrong.
Sympathise with why they held it.
Show where the old belief fails them.
Prove the new belief with a fact or demonstration.
Sell the product from the new belief.

test.method: Run belief-shift copy against a plain rebuttal line for the same objection.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Preface a real objection early so a fitting skimmer does not leave, keep the full FAQ at the bottom
hypothesis: If a likely objection is prefaced gently early in the page or email while the complete FAQ stays at the very bottom, then fewer good-fit skimmers leave early because their doubt is acknowledged before they scroll away, without cluttering the top with a full objection list.

signal.check: A likely early objection is never addressed until deep in the FAQ, and skimmers who share that doubt may leave before reaching it.

risk.note: A placement choice.

prerequisites: The store's most common early objection
steps: Identify the objection most likely to make a good-fit visitor leave early.
Write a soft preface line near the top that names it without stating it as settled fact ('Most people think X only works if...').
Move the complete FAQ, with every objection, to the very bottom for people who scroll straight down.
Let testimonials each answer one objection, spread through the page.

test.method: Check bounce rate on the page before and after the early preface line is added.
test.read_point: After a comparable traffic window post-change.

title: Address the 3 blockers for a warm list: risk, price, effectiveness
hypothesis: If emails to a store's own list address risk, price, and effectiveness rather than re-explaining what the product is, then warm subscribers convert more because these are the actual blockers holding back someone who already knows the product.

signal.check: List emails skip straight to a discount with no line on risk (returns, guarantee), price (value framing), or effectiveness (how and why it works).

risk.note: A content-checklist addition.

steps: Check the draft for a line addressing risk (return policy, guarantee).
Check for a line addressing price (value, not just discount).
Check for a line addressing effectiveness (how and why the product works, what it does differently).
Add whichever of the 3 is missing before the email sends.

test.method: Run an email covering all 3 blockers against a discount-only version to the same list segment.
test.read_point: After each send reaches a comparable list size.

title: Don't try to handle every objection in one email
hypothesis: If each email handles only one or two objections instead of every known objection, then the email stays short and readable because too much objection handling can make even a 288-word email feel long.

signal.check: A single email tries to answer 3 or more distinct objections at once, making it run long.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one source's heuristic finds too much objection handling makes a 288-word email feel long

risk.note: An editing check.

steps: Count the distinct objections addressed in the draft.
If there are more than 1 or 2, split the extra objections into their own emails.
Keep each email focused on its one idea and its one or two objections.

test.method: Compare click and read-through on a focused single-objection email against a multi-objection email.
test.read_point: After each send reaches a comparable list size.

title: Pre-empt a rival's pitch with true facts, using a weak attack only
hypothesis: If copy tells the buyer what to look for before they see a rival's pitch, using only true facts and a weak version of the counter-argument, then the brand holds the sale because inoculation works with legitimate facts and a genuinely better product, without crossing into a named attack.
does_not_apply_when: No verified, true difference exists to warn the buyer about

signal.check: The category has a well-known competing claim that the brand never addresses before the buyer encounters it elsewhere.

risk.note: Combine with the no-named-rival rule; use only verified facts, never an attack on a named brand.

prerequisites: A verified, true point of difference from competing claims
steps: Identify the competing claim buyers commonly hear elsewhere in the category.
Write a weak version of that counter-claim into the copy, then answer it with a true fact.
Never name a specific rival brand in this warning.

test.method: Run the pre-emptive version against a version with no mention of the competing claim.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Give every asset exactly one labeled call to action
hypothesis: If every ad, email, or page section carries exactly one labeled action, then more readers act because confusion from multiple asks is the biggest enemy of a click, unless the asset's whole job is 'shop the range', where a product grid counts as one action.

signal.check: An asset has more than one distinct type of ask (buy, follow, read more, sign up) competing for attention.

risk.note: A P.S. soft sell or a double CTA repeating the same ask is allowed.

steps: List every distinct ask in the current draft.
Cut all but one; a product grid counts as one action only if the whole email's job is 'shop the range'.
Label the single CTA with the exact store action it triggers (add to cart, shop now, get yours).

test.method: Run a single-CTA version against a multi-ask version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Tell people what to do, positively, and label what happens next
hypothesis: If the CTA states the action positively and labels what happens after the click, then more people click because a bare button like 'Start now' gets ignored when the reader has no idea what is behind it.

signal.check: The CTA is a bare, generic label ('Start now', 'Learn more') with no hint of what happens next.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one cited heatmap case found a bare 'Start now' button drew no clicks

risk.note: A CTA wording fix.

steps: State the action positively ('Order now', 'Send now for your sample') rather than a vague verb.
Add a short label of the outcome ('Order now, ships today') where space allows.
Assume the reader will act; do not hedge the ask.

test.method: Run the labeled CTA against the bare button version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Let the CTA say what to do; save how it works for after the click
hypothesis: If the CTA states only the action while the how (mechanism, process, details) is saved for the page behind the click, then the ask stays clean because the copy has already hinted at the how earlier, and the CTA does not need to re-explain it.

signal.check: The CTA button or line tries to explain the mechanism instead of just stating the action.

risk.note: A wording split, not a claim risk.

prerequisites: A mechanism hint already given earlier in the copy (R40)
steps: Check the CTA line for any explanation of how the product or offer works.
Move that explanation earlier in the copy, ahead of the CTA.
Keep the CTA itself to the plain action.

test.method: Compare click-through on a plain-action CTA against a CTA that tries to explain the mechanism.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Match the CTA's landing page to the ad's exact promise
hypothesis: If the page behind the CTA repeats the ad's promise in new words with a similar look, then fewer clicks bounce because congruency is cited as the biggest problem with paid ads and a mismatched landing page reads as a bait and switch.

signal.check: Clicking the ad lands on a page (like the home page) that does not clearly repeat the ad's specific promise.

risk.note: Requires coordinating the landing page copy; page build itself is 07-LPG's.

prerequisites: The ad's exact promise and the landing page it points to
steps: Write down the ad's exact promise in one line.
Check the first screen of the destination page repeats that promise in new words.
If the destination is the home page or an unrelated page, change the destination or rewrite the first screen.

test.method: Click through the live ad and check the landing page's first screen against the ad's promise.
test.read_point: Before the ad set ships, and again after launch.

title: Place a CTA or price block every 2 to 3 sections on a long page
hypothesis: If a long page places a CTA or price block every 2 to 3 content sections and ends with a P.S. or restated offer, then fewer ready-to-buy readers scroll past the chance to act because the next step is always nearby.

signal.check: A long page has only one CTA at the very top or bottom, with several sections of content in between and no chance to act.

risk.note: A layout-of-words addition.

steps: Count the content sections on the page.
Insert a CTA or price block after every 2 to 3 sections.
End the page with a P.S. or a final restated offer.

test.method: Check scroll depth and CTA clicks by position before and after adding mid-page CTAs.
test.read_point: After a comparable traffic window post-change.

title: Keep voice consistent across every SKU and collection page, checked 3 pages at a time
hypothesis: If voice is checked across 3 product pages side by side, not just one at a time, then the brand reads as one confident voice because a tone that shifts page to page never builds the same confidence a consistent one does.

signal.check: Product or collection pages read as written by different people, with no shared phrases from the brand's compile document.

risk.note: A QA check.

prerequisites: The brand's compile document (R10)
steps: Pull up 3 product or collection pages side by side, not just the one being edited.
Check tone, phrasing and persona match across all 3.
Rewrite any page whose phrasing drifts from the compile document's approved language, without turning bullets into repeated boilerplate.

test.method: Have someone read 3 pages back to back and flag any that feels like a different brand.
test.read_point: Before pages ship.

title: Default to positive framing; use negative framing only when the product fully resolves it
hypothesis: If copy defaults to a positive, result-shown frame and uses a negative frame only when the product fully removes the problem, without picturing the afflicted state or attaching the brand to it, then response holds up because positive framing outpulled negative 4 to 1 in cited keyed tests, while an unresolved negative frame risks looking like fear with no fix.

signal.check: The draft leads with a vivid negative scene (the 'before', the afflicted state) with the brand pictured inside it, or fear with no clear fix shown.

expected_effect.size: positive framing outpulled negative 4 to 1 in one set of keyed print tests

risk.note: Fear only works with a specific threat, a specific fix, proof the fix works, and proof the reader can do it; never all 4 missing.

steps: Check whether the current frame is positive (shows the result) or negative (shows the problem).
If negative, confirm the product fully resolves the problem shown; if not, switch to positive.
Never show the afflicted state as the centerpiece, and never place the brand inside a heavy negative scene.
If fear is used, include all 4 parts: the threat, the specific fix, proof the fix works, proof the reader can do it.

test.method: Run a positive-framed variant against a negative-framed variant of the same claim.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches comparable volume.

title: Put a real, named person behind founder-led copy, never an invented authority
hypothesis: If a founder-led or expert-led brand puts a real, named person's voice behind its copy, then trust rises because a real person talking beats a soulless corporate voice, as long as no authority is ever invented.
does_not_apply_when: A brand with no real founder or expert voice to use

signal.check: The brand has a real founder or expert but copy is written as a faceless company voice, or an invented expert persona appears with no real person behind it.

risk.note: Never invent an authority or persona with no real person behind it.

prerequisites: A willing, real founder or expert on the brand
steps: Identify the real founder or expert who can front the copy.
Write in their real voice, using the compile document's phrases.
Never attribute the copy to an invented persona with no real person behind it.

test.method: Run a founder-voiced version against the faceless-brand version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable volume.

title: Write like talking to a friend; cut jargon, school-essay grammar and AI tells
hypothesis: If copy is written the way you would say it to a friend, with jargon and known AI-tell phrases cut, then it reads as more human because phrases like 'take your business to the next level' or a double dash signal machine-written text that readers now recognise and discount.

signal.check: The draft has jargon, SAT words, school-essay grammar, or known AI tells (‘revolutionize', ‘don't miss out', an em dash, a double dash).

risk.note: An editing pass.

steps: Scan for jargon and SAT words; replace with plain, everyday words.
Scan for known AI tells (revolutionize, don't miss out, magic-wand analogies, double dashes) and cut them.
Read the line aloud and check it sounds like something you would say to a friend, not an essay.

test.method: Scan the final draft against a running list of AI-tell phrases and cut every match before shipping.
test.read_point: During the editing pass.

title: Limit emojis to 1 or 2 in an email, only more in a social caption if the persona uses them
hypothesis: If emails carry at most 1 or 2 emojis and a social caption uses more only when the brand's persona already does, then the tone stays consistent because heavy emoji use clashes with a calm or serious persona.

signal.check: An email or caption uses several emojis when the brand's compile document shows a calm, serious, or no-nonsense persona.

risk.note: Current emoji norms should be checked; a 2019 source's note that emojis pulled in ads is dated.

prerequisites: The brand's voice samples
steps: Count emojis in the draft.
For an email, cap at 1 or 2.
For a social caption, use more only if the brand's own past posts already use them that way.

test.method: Compare click and reply rates on a low-emoji version against a heavy-emoji version, matched to the persona.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable sends.

title: Don't qualify the reader into a narrow slice unless the send is actually segmented
hypothesis: If a hook or subject line does not narrow the reader into a slice ('if you're 40ish') unless that exact send is already segmented to that slice, then fewer eligible buyers feel excluded because a qualifier aimed at nobody in particular quietly turns away people who would have bought.

signal.check: A hook or subject line names a narrow slice of buyers ('for busy moms only') while the send goes to the full, unsegmented list or audience.

risk.note: A targeting-copy match check.

prerequisites: Knowledge of whether this exact send is segmented
steps: Check if the audience for this send is actually filtered to the slice the hook names.
If not segmented, broaden the hook to fit the whole audience.
Only keep a narrow qualifier when the audience list is genuinely that narrow.

test.method: Compare response on a narrow-qualifier hook against a broad hook, sent to the same unsegmented audience.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable sends.

title: Rest the draft, then read it aloud until it doesn't stumble
hypothesis: If a draft rests for at least a walk, ideally 24 hours, before a final read-aloud pass with fixes restarting from the top on any stumble, then more errors and awkward lines get caught because fresh eyes and ears notice what the writer's tired brain skips over.

signal.check: A draft is edited and shipped in the same sitting it was written, with no rest and no read-aloud pass.

risk.note: A scheduling and process step.

prerequisites: Enough lead time before the deadline to allow a rest period
steps: Finish the draft, then step away: 24 hours if the schedule allows, otherwise at least a short walk.
Read the whole piece aloud.
On any stumble, fix it and restart the read-aloud from the top.
Ship only once a full read-aloud passes with no stumble.

test.method: Track how many rounds of read-aloud it takes before a draft passes clean, and whether rested drafts need fewer rounds.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Cut every word that isn't working with a modifier sweep and the burrito test
hypothesis: If every draft is swept for weak modifiers, doubled words and repeated sentences, and each paragraph is tested by pulling one sentence to see if it still works, then the copy tightens because a word or sentence that is not working for you is working against you.

signal.check: The draft has filler words ('very', 'really', 'almost', 'barely'), doubled words, or repeated sentences that survived to the final version.

risk.note: An editing pass.

steps: Scan for 'very', 'really', 'almost', 'barely' and cut or replace with a real number.
Scan for doubled words and repeated sentences and cut.
For each paragraph, pull out 1 sentence; if the paragraph still works, that sentence should not have been there.

test.method: Count filler words per 100 words before and after the sweep.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Cut the lead and move the best line to the top
hypothesis: If the opening lines of an email or ad are cut and the strongest line in the body is moved to the top, then more readers keep reading because a slow wind-up delays the value a reader is scanning for.

signal.check: The first few lines of the draft build up to a point instead of stating it, while a stronger line sits further down in the body.

expected_effect.size: unknown; cutting the lead is the starting point for about 80 percent of one editor's critiques

risk.note: An editing pass.

steps: Read the first 3 to 4 lines and identify any wind-up with no payoff.
Find the strongest line anywhere in the draft.
Move that line to the top and cut the wind-up entirely.

test.method: Run the edited, lead-cut version against the original opening as 2 variants.
test.read_point: After each variant reaches comparable spend or sends.

title: Run the tossed salad audit: cut any claim that doesn't serve the one idea
hypothesis: If every claim in a draft is listed and any not serving the asset's one idea is cut or rewritten, then the argument reads clearer because a stranger should be able to state the argument in one sentence, and a divergent claim breaks that test.

signal.check: The draft has a claim that does not connect to the asset's stated one idea, added because it seemed like a good point on its own.

risk.note: An editing-pass audit.

prerequisites: The one idea stated in P2
steps: List every claim in the draft.
Flag any claim that is not a sub-point of the stated one idea.
Cut or rewrite each flagged claim.
Have a stranger state the argument back in 1 sentence as a final check.

test.method: Ask someone unfamiliar with the brief to state the draft's argument in one sentence.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Score readability in code and shorten words and sentences until it passes
hypothesis: If readability is scored with a Flesch calculation run in code rather than judged by eye, then the copy reliably hits the reading floor because a model's own estimate of grade level is not trustworthy without a computed check.

signal.check: No readability score is computed for the draft, or the score is an eyeballed guess rather than a code-run calculation.

expected_effect.size: target 70 or higher, which maps to 7th grade or easier on the Flesch scale

risk.note: Compute in code; never trust the model's own estimate.

prerequisites: A Flesch or readability scoring script
steps: Run the draft through a Flesch Reading Ease calculation in code.
If the score is below 70, shorten sentences and swap in shorter words.
Re-score after each pass until it clears 70 and stays below the tenth-grade ecomOS floor.

test.method: Log the Flesch score for every asset before it ships and track the average over time.
test.read_point: Before every asset ships.

title: Overwrite then cut, get outside feedback, hold a 9-of-10 ship bar
hypothesis: If key lines are drafted in 4 or 5 versions, shown to a reviewer after 2 to 3 hours of solo work, and shipped only at a 9-of-10 bar, then quality rises because working alone past that point loses judgement and a fresh reviewer catches what the writer no longer sees.

signal.check: A key headline or hook ships as the first version written, with no alternate versions drafted and no outside review.

risk.note: A process discipline.

prerequisites: A second reviewer available
steps: Write 4 or 5 versions of the key line.
Show 3 of the strongest to a reviewer.
Get outside feedback once 2 to 3 hours have been spent alone on the asset.
Ship only when you would rate it 9 out of 10; if you would not, keep cutting.

test.method: Track how many versions were drafted and whether outside feedback was collected before each ship.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Run the skim test: scroll without reading and check the offer still lands
hypothesis: If a page or email is scrolled quickly without reading closely, and the offer still comes through from the bold and short lines alone, then real skimming readers convert more because most readers scan before they ever commit to reading in full.

signal.check: Scrolling the draft quickly leaves no clear sense of the offer; the message only comes through if every line is read in full.

risk.note: A QA check, not a content risk.

steps: Scroll through the finished draft quickly without reading each line.
Note whether the offer, the benefit and the CTA are still clear from bold and short lines alone.
Add or bolden a scroll-stopper line anywhere the skim leaves a gap.
Left-align body text; never centre small text.

test.method: Have someone unfamiliar with the draft skim it for 5 seconds and describe the offer.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Match the subject or headline to the body, and write the preview by hand
hypothesis: If the subject line matches the body's actual angle and the preview text is written by hand instead of auto-filled, then open-to-read continuity holds because a mismatched subject or an auto-filled preview breaks the promise that got the open.

signal.check: The subject line promises a different angle than the body delivers, or the preview text is left to auto-fill from the first line.

risk.note: A pre-send check.

steps: Read the subject line and the body's actual angle and check they match.
Write the preview text by hand so it adds to the subject instead of repeating it.
Never refer back to the subject line inside the body ('as I said in the subject').

test.method: Check subject, preview and body angle against each other before every send.
test.read_point: Before the send.

title: Write and check copy in its real surface, not a blank document
hypothesis: If copy is written and checked directly in a mock-up of the real ad, email or page, then line wraps and truncation match what the reader actually sees, because writing in a blank document and pasting in later lets bad wraps and cut-off promises slip through.

signal.check: Copy is drafted entirely in a plain document and pasted into the live surface only at the very end, with no preview check.

risk.note: A process check requiring the preview tool for each placement.

prerequisites: A preview tool or mock-up for the placement
steps: Draft or move the copy into the real surface (ad preview, email template, page builder) before finalising.
Check line wraps, truncation points, and how it sits beside the image.
Shorten by cutting filler words, never by cutting the specific claim, if a line runs long.

test.method: Preview the final copy in the live tool and check nothing is cut mid-promise.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Send a value email before the next promo instead of chaining promos
hypothesis: If at least one value email goes out between promotions instead of sending promo after promo, then list fatigue and unsubscribes drop because a list that only ever hears asks has no goodwill deposit to draw on.

signal.check: Send history shows 2 or more promotional sends in a row with no value-only email between them.

risk.note: A cadence check within email copy planning; flow timing itself belongs to 14-EML.

prerequisites: Send history for the list
steps: Check send history for the last 2 to 3 sends before planning the next promo.
If the last sends were promotional, plan a value-only email first.
Confirm the value email gives something real (a tip, a story, a resource) with no ask attached.

test.method: Compare unsubscribe rate and click rate on a promo preceded by a value email versus back-to-back promos.
test.read_point: After the next 2 promo cycles.

title: Fetch the live Meta character limits and truncation points before writing to them
hypothesis: If the current Meta character limits and truncation points are fetched fresh before every launch-ready set, then the copy stops getting cut mid-promise because no source gives these figures and the platform changes them without notice.

signal.check: The team writes ad copy to a remembered or old character limit instead of checking the current Meta ad specs page before this launch.

risk.note: A pre-launch check; re-verify before every launch-ready set.

prerequisites: Access to the current Meta ad specs page
steps: Check the current Meta ad specs page for primary text, headline and description limits and the 'see more' truncation point, per placement.
Write the payoff before that truncation point.
Re-check on every new launch-ready set, since the platform can change these without notice.

test.method: Preview the finished ad in the platform's own tool and confirm nothing important falls after 'see more'.
test.read_point: Before every launch-ready set.

title: Follow email format rules: short subject, hand-written preview, text-led body
hypothesis: If every email keeps its subject at 40 characters or fewer with no ending period, writes the preview by hand, and lets words carry the message with images added only where they add meaning, then more of the send reads as intended because a heavy template or an ambiguous subject can clip or confuse before the message lands.

signal.check: A subject line runs over 40 characters, ends in a period, or the email is built as an image-heavy template with the words doing little of the work.

risk.note: Deliverability and clipping limits should be checked live; they change with client rules.

steps: Count the subject line's characters and trim to 40 or fewer, with no ending period.
Write the preview text by hand rather than letting it auto-fill.
Write the email so the words alone carry the message with images turned off; add images only where they add real meaning, not decoration.
Keep story and value emails to about 200 to 300 words unless the email has one short job.

test.method: Check subject character count and preview text by hand before every send, and compare a text-led email against an image-heavy one.
test.read_point: Before the send, then after comparable sends of each format.

title: Assemble the page hero as eyebrow, headline, deck and one CTA
hypothesis: If the page hero always follows eyebrow (who it is for), headline (the promise), deck (ease, time frame or guarantee), and one CTA, then the first screen answers who, why keep reading, and what to do next, because that 4-part order covers all 3 questions a new visitor asks.

signal.check: The page hero is missing one of the 4 parts (no eyebrow naming who it's for, no deck easing the ask, or more than one CTA) and a new visitor could not say who it's for from the top of the page.

risk.note: Page layout and build stay with 07-LPG; this covers the words.

prerequisites: The headline from the bank (R30) and the offer or guarantee terms
steps: Write the eyebrow naming who the page is for.
Use the top headline promise as the hero headline.
Write a deck line adding ease, a time frame, or a guarantee.
Add exactly one CTA.

test.method: Show only the hero to someone unfamiliar with the page and ask who it's for and what to do next.
test.read_point: Before the page ships.

title: Treat a 1-element ad (headline-only, image-only, or logo-only) as a test, not a default
hypothesis: If a static ad carried by just 1 element (only the headline, only the picture, or only the logo) is run as a deliberate test variant rather than the account's default format, then the account avoids losing product identity in most of its ads while still learning whether the minimal format can work.

signal.check: A 1-element ad format has become the default template for the account rather than one tested variant among several fuller-identity ads.

risk.note: A 1-element ad risks failing the product-identity check; keep it to 1 of several variants, not the default.

steps: Check whether the account defaults to a 1-element ad format for every set.
If so, run it as 1 of 3 variants, with the others showing product, promise and brand together.
Compare cost per purchase between the 1-element variant and the fuller-identity variants.

test.method: Run a 1-element variant against 2 fuller-identity variants in the same ad set.
test.read_point: After the ad set reaches enough spend to compare variants.

title: Write SMS as one short line: the offer or update, a clear action, and the opt-out
hypothesis: If SMS copy stays to one short line with the offer or update, a clear action, and the opt-out or help instruction required by law, then sends stay compliant and readable because SMS has no room for a fuller argument and carries its own legal requirements.

signal.check: An SMS send runs long, lacks a clear single action, or omits the opt-out or help instruction required by the carrier or local law.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data and current SMS compliance rules before use

risk.note: Missing the required opt-out or help instruction is a compliance risk, not just a style issue.

prerequisites: Current SMS compliance rules for the brand's market
steps: State the offer or update in one short line.
Add one clear action (a link or a reply instruction).
Include the opt-out or help instruction the carrier and local law require.
Check current SMS compliance rules for the brand's market before sending.

test.method: Check every SMS draft against the required opt-out and help wording before it sends.
test.read_point: Before the SMS sends.

title: Front-load a marketplace listing title with product, key spec and use case
hypothesis: If a marketplace listing title leads with the product, its key spec, and the use case in the platform's expected order, then more shoppers find and click it because marketplace search ranks and displays titles by that front-loaded structure.

signal.check: A marketplace listing title buries the product type or key spec after brand name or filler words, out of the platform's expected order.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data and the marketplace's current listing rules before use

risk.note: Check the marketplace's current title and bullet rules before use.

prerequisites: The marketplace's current listing title format rules
steps: Check the platform's expected title order (product, brand, key spec, use case, or its own variant).
Rewrite the title to front-load the product, key spec and use case in that order.
Write bullets as short, keyword-led claims, each sourced to the brand record.

test.method: Compare search impressions and click-through before and after the title reorder.
test.read_point: After a comparable traffic window post-change.

title: Never invent a statistic, quote, test count, review count or 'as seen in' claim
hypothesis: If every number, study, quote, count or 'as seen in' line traces to the brand record or a source the writer has actually opened, then the account avoids a policy strike or a boomeranged claim because an invented statistic is a permanent risk no craft benefit outweighs.

signal.check: A draft includes a statistic, study, quote, review count, customer count or savings figure with no traceable source in the brand record or an opened document.

risk.note: This is an absolute ecomOS rule that overrides any source suggesting invented proof or 'stats from Google or an LLM'.

steps: List every number, quote, study reference and count in the draft.
For each, name its exact source: a brand record field, a document, or a source the writer opened.
Cut or rewrite as a plain fact anything with no traceable source.
Never accept a statistic an AI tool supplies without an opened source behind it.

test.method: Check every number and quote in the final draft against a named source before it ships.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Verify every impressive claim against a document or test before it runs
hypothesis: If every factual claim is backed by a source the writer has actually seen and impressive claims are verified before launch, then the brand avoids a boomeranged claim because an unverified but impressive-sounding line can bar the ad once it is checked.

signal.check: An impressive number, comparison, or performance claim ships with no document or test result on file confirming it.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a cited historical case turned an unverified 'large food value' claim into a lab-confirmed 425 calories per pint

risk.note: An unverified claim that later proves false can bar the ad and damage trust.

prerequisites: A document, lab result, or test that can confirm the claim
steps: List every factual claim in the draft.
For each, write the source: a link to the original document, a lab result, or a source the writer opened.
Verify any impressive or surprising claim against that source before the asset runs.
Cut any claim with no document behind it.

test.method: Check each impressive claim against its cited document before the asset ships.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Check every claim type against current platform policy before launch
hypothesis: If health, weight, income, before-and-after, safety, personal-attribute, 'free', urgency and comparative claims are each checked against current platform and consumer-protection rules before launch, then the ad account avoids a policy strike because these categories move often and a claim allowed last month may be restricted now.

signal.check: A launch-ready set includes a health, income, before-and-after, or urgency claim with no record of a current policy check.

risk.note: A policy strike can pause or ban the ad account; re-check monthly for these categories.

prerequisites: Access to current Meta advertising standards and local consumer-protection rules
steps: List every claim in the set by type: health, weight, income, before and after, safety, personal attributes, 'free', urgency, comparative.
Check each type against the current platform advertising standards.
Check urgency and 'free' claims against local consumer-protection rules.
Remove or rewrite any claim that fails the current check.

test.method: Log the policy page and date checked for each claim type before every launch-ready set.
test.read_point: Before every launch-ready set.

title: Keep testimonials real, permitted in writing, and unedited in meaning
hypothesis: If every testimonial used is real, has written permission on file, and is never edited to change its meaning, then the brand avoids an endorsement-rule violation because using a testimonial without permission or editing its meaning is a compliance and trust risk.

signal.check: A testimonial appears in copy with no permission record on file, or its wording has been changed from what the customer actually said.

risk.note: Check current endorsement and review rules for the brand's country and each platform.

prerequisites: A permission record for each testimonial used
steps: Confirm written permission is on file for every testimonial used.
Check the quoted text matches what the customer actually said, with no meaning changed.
Disclose any incentive given for the testimonial, as the market requires.
Remove any testimonial missing permission until it is fixed.

test.method: Check the permission file for every testimonial before it ships.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Match guarantee wording exactly to the brand record's eligibility limits
hypothesis: If guarantee copy states the term, what qualifies and how to claim exactly as the brand record allows, then customers and operations stay aligned because a guarantee written broader than the real policy creates disputes operations cannot honour.

signal.check: Guarantee copy in an ad, page or email is broader or vaguer than the brand record's actual eligibility limits.

risk.note: Never promise a term or eligibility broader than what operations can honour.

prerequisites: The exact guarantee policy and eligibility limits from the brand record
steps: Pull the exact guarantee term and eligibility limits from the brand record.
Compare the draft's guarantee wording line by line against the record.
Rewrite any line that overstates the term, the eligibility, or how to claim it.

test.method: Check the shipped guarantee wording against the brand record before every launch.
test.read_point: Before the asset ships.

title: Quote the exact page, price and date behind every claim that names a number or promise
hypothesis: If every ad that names a price, price cap, count, policy or delivery promise carries a claim-check line quoting the exact page title, the value as shown, and the date it was read, then wrong-price and stale-claim errors drop because a specific claim can be checked back against the exact page it came from.

signal.check: An ad names a price, price cap, count or delivery promise with no record of which page and value it was checked against, or when.

expected_effect.size: unknown; added after a copy test where a wrong price-cap headline cost the round

risk.note: A price-cap headline must match the landing page's own title or filter exactly, not a rounded or nearby number.

prerequisites: The exact landing page or filter the ad points to
steps: For every ad naming a price, price cap, count, policy or delivery promise, open the exact page it refers to.
Write the claim-check line: page title as shown, value as shown, date read.
Confirm a reader could open the page and see the same words the ad uses.

test.method: Open the cited page and confirm the value in the ad matches exactly, on the date logged.
test.read_point: Before every launch, and again if the page could have changed.

title: Never leave a blank placeholder in client-facing copy
hypothesis: If every unknown date, code, price or count is written as an explicit 'confirm before launch' note instead of a blank or 'XX', then nothing ships half-finished because a document with a hidden blank looks finished when it is not.

signal.check: A client document has a blank space, 'XX', 'TBD' or an underscore standing in for a date, code, price or count.

risk.note: A pre-handoff check.

steps: Search the document for '[ ]', 'XX', 'TBD' and underscores before hand-off.
Replace any found with an explicit '[confirm before launch: what]' note.
Never hand off a client document with a blank still in it.

test.method: Grep the final document for '[ ]', 'XX', 'TBD' and underscores before every hand-off.
test.read_point: Before hand-off.

title: Run a full claim audit table before every set ships
hypothesis: If every set goes through a claim audit table listing each claim, its type, its source, whether it's verified, its policy check, any arithmetic and the action taken, then nothing unsupported reaches the account because the audit forces a source or a cut for every single claim before launch.

signal.check: A set ships with no claim audit table on file listing each claim's source, verification status and policy check.

risk.note: The audit process itself; each individual claim check is a separate risk covered by other ideas.

prerequisites: The finished draft and the brand record's approved and banned claims lists
steps: List every claim in the draft: numbers, comparisons, outcomes, times, counts, certifications, 'free', guarantees, deadlines, quotes, testimonials, superlatives, figurative lines.
For each, record the source, whether it's verified, the policy check and date, any arithmetic, and the action (kept, rewritten, removed).
Check every figurative line against the reasonable-reader test: would it be taken as a literal spec, time, count or outcome?
Write a 1-line verdict: ready, or blocked on named claims.

test.method: Check the claim audit table is complete and every row has a source or an action before launch.
test.read_point: Before every launch-ready set.

title: Give each ad variant one genuinely different angle, never a synonym swap
hypothesis: If each of 3 ad variants carries a genuinely different angle (a different benefit, moment, objection or execution) instead of the same idea reworded, then the test actually learns something because comparing synonyms of the same angle tells the team nothing new.

signal.check: The 3 variants in an ad set differ only in wording, not in the underlying benefit, moment, objection or execution.

risk.note: A planning step before drafting.

prerequisites: A list of candidate benefits, moments, objections and executions
steps: Before drafting, list 3 genuinely different angles: a benefit, a customer moment, an objection, or an execution.
Assign one angle per variant before writing any copy.
Check the finished variants against each other; if 2 collapse into the same angle, replace 1 with the next angle on the list.

test.method: Have someone unfamiliar with the brief name each variant's angle; check all 3 differ.
test.read_point: Before the ad set ships, then after it reaches enough spend.

title: Change one variable per test and judge it by cost per purchase, not clicks or opens
hypothesis: If a test changes exactly one variable and is judged by cost per purchase or conversion rate rather than clicks or opens, then the result is trustworthy because changing several things at once, or judging by clicks, hides which change actually mattered.

signal.check: A live test changes more than one element at a time (headline and image and offer), or the team is judging results by CTR or open rate instead of cost per purchase.

risk.note: A test-design discipline.

steps: Name the single variable this test changes.
Keep every other element constant between the control and the variant.
Judge the result by cost per purchase or purchase conversion rate, using CTR only as a selection signal, never the goal.
Keep one control method running for at least a set period before drawing a conclusion.

test.method: Log the one changed variable and compare cost per purchase between control and variant.
test.read_point: After the test reaches enough spend or sends, sized from the brand's own traffic.

title: When an ad fails, change the headline first, then check price, then change the offer
hypothesis: If a failing ad is rescued by changing the headline first, then checking price against the market, then changing the offer, then the fix targets the highest-leverage element first because a headline change alone has swung keyed results 5 to 10 times.

signal.check: A launched ad with poor results gets its offer or price changed first, before the headline has been tested.

expected_effect.size: a headline change alone swung keyed print results 5 to 10 times in one source's account

risk.note: A rescue-order discipline.

prerequisites: Results data for the failing ad
steps: Write a fresh headline bank for the failing ad and test it first.
If the headline change does not fix it, check the price against the current market.
If price is not the issue, change the offer last.

test.method: Track cost per purchase after each successive change (headline, then price check, then offer) to see which fixed it.
test.read_point: After each change reaches enough spend to judge.

title: Keep a proven winner running until its own numbers decline; then swap execution, not the appeal
hypothesis: If a winning ad keeps running until its own results decline, and any change then keeps the winning appeal, claim and offer while swapping only the execution, then spend is not wasted refreshing a working ad out of boredom, because Mead famously would not change a word of a proven ad for $10,000.

signal.check: A working ad is replaced or refreshed on a fixed schedule or because the team is tired of it, with no decline in its own results.

risk.note: Frequency and fatigue reads for a small retargeting audience belong to 24-DEP; a small audience does tire faster than a large cold audience.

prerequisites: Ad-level results over time, with frequency and reach
steps: Track the winning ad's own cost per purchase over time.
Leave it running as long as its own numbers hold, regardless of how long it has run.
On a measured decline, keep the same appeal, claim and offer; change only the execution (image, format, first line).
Add new angles as additions to the mix, not replacements for the winner.

test.method: Track the winning ad's cost per purchase weekly and only change it after a clear, sustained decline.
test.read_point: Weekly, comparing against the ad's own trailing baseline.

title: Weight the ad mix by proven pull, keeping any appeal that still pays at half the best appeal's return
hypothesis: If spend is weighted toward appeals with proven pull, but an appeal is kept as long as it still pays at half the best appeal's return, then total account return improves because dropping every appeal but the top one narrows the audience the account can reach profitably.

signal.check: Spend is concentrated entirely on the single best-performing appeal with no data-informed mix across appeals with a proven, if lower, return.

risk.note: Needs the brand's own results by appeal.

prerequisites: Keyed results by appeal for the brand
steps: Rank appeals by their own cost per purchase or return, using the brand's own results.
Keep any appeal that still pays at half the best appeal's return.
Drop only appeals that fall below that half-of-best threshold.
Rebalance spend toward the strongest appeals without cutting the still-paying ones entirely.

test.method: Compare account-level cost per purchase before and after rebalancing spend by this rule.
test.read_point: After a full spend cycle under the new mix.

title: Size copy tests from the brand's own traffic and volume, not a fixed rule
hypothesis: If test size and duration are set from the brand's own traffic and conversion volume instead of a borrowed rule of thumb, then test results are trustworthy because no source in this playbook gives a real test-size or significance rule for copy tests.

signal.check: A copy test is called a winner or loser after an arbitrary time or spend with no check against the brand's own traffic volume for statistical reliability.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a copy-test size or duration rule

risk.note: Hand the sizing question to 09-CRO if the brand needs a formal significance rule.

prerequisites: Traffic and conversion volume data for the test surface
steps: Check the brand's own traffic and conversion volume for the surface being tested.
Size the test's spend or send volume and duration from that real volume, not a fixed industry rule.
If the brand needs a formal significance threshold, hand the sizing question to 09-CRO.

test.method: Check the test ran long enough, at enough spend or sends, to reach a reliable read given the brand's own volume.
test.read_point: Before declaring a test result final.

title: Study the brand's own winners first, then study close competitors one at a time
hypothesis: If the brand's own past winning ads are studied and ranked by cost per purchase before any competitor is analysed, and competitors are each studied one at a time rather than pooled, then the next set improves faster because pooling multiple competitors together dilutes the pattern to a generic average.

signal.check: A new copy job starts by looking at competitor ads before the brand's own past results have been reviewed, or several competitors are analysed together in one pass.

risk.note: A research-order discipline.

prerequisites: Past ad copy with spend and results for the brand
steps: Rank the brand's own past ads by cost per purchase, or by CTR at matched spend if cost per purchase is unavailable.
Ask whether the past winners were single-idea and specific.
Only after that, study close competitors, one brand per analysis run, never pooled.
Record layout and structure notes only from competitor ads; never save their text as copy.

test.method: Check the research order followed: brand's own winners first, competitors analysed one at a time after.
test.read_point: Before the next set is drafted.

title: Record every delivered set: brief, idea, angles, claims and sources, cards used, and later the result
hypothesis: If every delivered copy set is recorded with its brief, idea, angle per variant, claim sources and later result, then future decisions about winners, appeals and studies improve because R118, R119 and R121 all depend on having this history to draw from.

signal.check: A delivered set has no record of its brief, idea, angles, or claim sources once it ships, making later performance review or reuse impossible.

risk.note: A record-keeping step, not a claim risk.

steps: For every delivered set, record the brief, the one idea, and the angle per variant.
Record the claims used and their sources, and the cards used.
Record the date.
Add the result field once performance data is available.

test.method: Check that every delivered set in the last month has a complete record on file.
test.read_point: Monthly review of delivered sets.

title: Let AI draft and improve lines, but never let it author copy or supply proof
hypothesis: If a human writes first and only lifts AI-suggested lines that beat the human draft, with every added fact or quote verified and AI tells stripped, then copy stays trustworthy and on-voice because letting AI author the copy or supply unverified proof is the single biggest way invented claims enter the pipeline.

signal.check: A draft is generated by AI first and edited afterward, rather than written by a human first with AI used only to improve specific lines, or an AI-added stat or quote has not been verified.

risk.note: An AI-supplied statistic or credential must never ship unverified.

steps: Write the draft by hand first, before asking AI for any version.
Use AI only to research, suggest improvements, or offer alternate lines.
Lift an AI-suggested line only if it beats the human draft.
Strip any AI tell and verify every fact or quote the AI adds before it ships.

test.method: Check whether the human draft existed before any AI draft, for a sample of recent assets.
test.read_point: Ongoing, spot-checked per project.

title: Reserve ALL CAPS for print packaging and inserts; avoid it in digital ads
hypothesis: If ALL CAPS is kept out of digital ads and used sparingly, only on print packaging or inserts, then reading speed holds up because a 1956 study found all-caps text slows reading by about 11.8 percent compared with mixed case.

signal.check: A digital ad, email or page uses ALL CAPS for emphasis on more than a short phrase.

expected_effect.size: all-caps text read about 11.8 percent slower than mixed case in a cited 1956 study

risk.note: Not applicable to screens; only relevant for physical packaging or inserts.

steps: Scan digital copy for ALL CAPS words or phrases.
Convert to mixed case, keeping emphasis through bold or a short phrase instead.
Reserve ALL CAPS, at most 4 to 5 words, for print packaging or inserts only.

test.method: Run a mixed-case version against an all-caps version of the same line.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable spend or sends.

title: Make plain benefit emails about 80 percent of sends; save gimmicks for the rest
hypothesis: If roughly 80 percent of email sends are plain, straightforward benefit emails with gimmicks kept to a minority, then the list stays receptive because one source's own practice runs plain benefit emails about 80 percent of the time and uses gimmicks only after the plain ones work.

signal.check: Recent sends lean heavily on gimmicks, cute formats or novelty structures instead of plain, benefit-led emails.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one source runs about 80 percent plain benefit emails in his own practice

risk.note: A send-mix planning guideline.

prerequisites: A record of recent send types
steps: Review the last 10 sends and count how many were plain benefit emails versus gimmick or novelty formats.
Plan the next batch of sends so plain benefit emails make up roughly 80 percent.
Use a gimmick format only after the plain emails are already performing.

test.method: Track the ratio of plain to gimmick sends over a month and compare click rate trends.
test.read_point: After a month of sends.

title: Check the Ads Library for competitor long-runners on a fixed weekly or twice-monthly cadence
hypothesis: If the Meta Ads Library is checked for competitor long-running ads on a fixed cadence (weekly or twice a month) instead of only before a new project, then the team catches format shifts sooner because a long-running ad is itself the signal that it is working for that competitor.

signal.check: The team only checks competitor ads when starting a new project, with no standing weekly or biweekly check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one source's practice observation, 2019, dated

risk.note: Layout and mood signal only; never copy competitor text.

prerequisites: Access to the Meta Ad Library
steps: Set a standing weekly or twice-monthly reminder to check the Ads Library for the brand's top competitors.
Note any new long-running ad and its format, not its exact wording.
Feed layout and mood notes into the next competitor audit (R14).

test.method: Check whether the standing cadence surfaced a competitor shift before the next full audit would have.
test.read_point: Monthly review of the watch log.

title: Offer an installment or bill-later payment framing for higher-priced items
hypothesis: If a higher-priced item's checkout copy offers an installment or bill-later framing instead of only the full price, then more buyers complete checkout because splitting the price or delaying payment has been claimed to add meaningfully to response versus a single upfront price.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no installment or bill-later payment mechanism available

signal.check: A high-priced item's checkout or page copy shows only the full upfront price with no installment or bill-later option mentioned, even though the payment provider supports one.

expected_effect.size: installments over $15 are claimed to add about 15 percent to response, and 'Bill Me' 50 percent or more, in one uncited source

risk.note: Requires a real installment or bill-later payment mechanism; word only what the checkout can actually offer.

prerequisites: An installment or bill-later payment provider integrated at checkout
steps: Confirm the brand's checkout supports an installment or bill-later option.
Add a line near the price showing the per-installment amount or the bill-later terms.
Verify the exact terms shown match what the payment provider offers.

test.method: Run a version with the installment framing shown against the current full-price-only version.
test.read_point: After each version reaches comparable order volume.

title: Test BOGO framing against an equivalent percent-off framing for the same discount
hypothesis: If the same discount value is offered as buy-one-get-one instead of an equivalent percent off, then response may rise because one uncited source's testing claims BOGO beats 50% off at the same underlying value.

signal.check: The brand always frames a 2-for-1-value discount as a percent off, and has never tested a BOGO framing of the same underlying value.

expected_effect.size: unknown; one source's uncited testing claim says BOGO beats 50 percent off

risk.note: The two framings must represent the same real discount value; compute the equivalence in code.

prerequisites: A product suited to being bought in twos
steps: Pick a product where a 2-for-1-value discount makes sense.
Compute the equivalent percent-off value for the same real discount, in code.
Run a BOGO-framed offer against the percent-off-framed offer of the same value.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and units per order between the BOGO and percent-off framings.
test.read_point: After each framing reaches comparable order volume.

title: Test a pay-after-trial framing against a standard money-back guarantee
hypothesis: If operations can support delaying payment until after a trial period, testing that framing against a standard money-back guarantee may convert more buyers because historical cases found pay-after-trial beat money-back guarantees many times over in older keyed tests.
does_not_apply_when: Operations cannot support delayed payment or invoicing after delivery

signal.check: The brand offers only a standard money-back guarantee and has never tested a pay-after-trial or pay-on-approval framing, despite having the operational ability to invoice after delivery.

expected_effect.size: unknown; historical 1920s cases cited pay-after-trial beating money-back guarantees, not verified for modern ecommerce

risk.note: Pay-after-trial carries real payment-collection risk; confirm operations and finance can support it before testing.

prerequisites: Finance and operations sign-off on a pay-after-trial or invoice-after-delivery mechanism
steps: Confirm with finance and operations whether pay-after-trial is operationally possible.
If yes, word the offer as try first, pay only if you keep it.
Run this framing against the standard money-back guarantee for the same product.

test.method: Compare conversion rate and non-payment or return rate between the pay-after-trial and money-back guarantee framings.
test.read_point: After each framing reaches comparable order volume and the payment window closes.

title: Avoid an 'Introducing [product]' launch email subject line
hypothesis: If a launch email's subject avoids the plain 'Introducing [product]' pattern, then open rate may hold up better because one source's list saw that pattern open around 15 percent versus a normal 25 to 30 percent.

signal.check: A launch email's subject line uses the literal 'Introducing:' or 'Introducing [product]' pattern with nothing else to earn the open.

expected_effect.size: an 'Introducing' subject opened about 15 percent versus a normal 25 to 30 percent on one dated list

risk.note: The figure is dated, from before Apple Mail Privacy Protection; check current open-rate reliability before relying on it.

steps: Check the launch email's subject line for the plain 'Introducing' pattern.
Rewrite it around the benefit or the buying question instead of the product announcement alone.
Keep 'Introducing: [product]' only as a deliberate exception when the brand wants to name the product on purpose.

test.method: Run a benefit-led subject against an 'Introducing' subject for the same launch, on a split list if volume allows.
test.read_point: After the send, though open-rate reliability should be treated with caution post-Apple Mail Privacy Protection.
